articles.title: Middle Eastern Concept De Babel Opens Second Scottsdale, Arizona
articles.titleKo: Middle Eastern Concept De Babel Opens Second Scottsdale, Arizona
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . De Babel is opening its second Scottsdale location at The Edge, introducing a distinctive format that brings together made-to-order Middle Eastern food, elevated hospitality and a carefully curated market of essential Middle Eastern products. Located at 8980 N. 90th St., Suite 124, the new restaurant preserves the familiar flavors, quality and consistency established at De Babel’s original Pima Road location. De Babel remains a strictly halal kitchen, with restaurant food preparation and made-to-order menu items following the brand’s halal standards. The Edge location expands the experience beyond the traditional fast-casual model. It offers large patios, comfortable soft seating and an environment designed to encourage guests to relax, gather and experience genuine Middle Eastern hospitality without sacrificing convenience. “We wanted to create a more complete experience while remaining true to who we are,” said De Babel founder Marwan Kandeel. “The food will continue to be made to order, the kitchen will remain strictly halal and our guests will still find the consistent flavors they know. At the same time, we are creating a more comfortable environment and making important Middle Eastern products easier to find.” A carefully curated Middle Eastern market The market features selected Pereg kosher products alongside Halloumi, Bulgarian, Akkawi and Nabulsi cheeses; Tahsildaroglu Goat’s Milk White cheese; tahini; pickles; and a wide assortment of gluten-free packaged products. Although the retail market carries selected kosher-certified packaged products, De Babel itself remains a strictly halal kitchen. The distinction allows the restaurant to maintain its halal menu while making thoughtfully selected packaged products available to guests with different dietary preferences. Organic beverages served differently Guests can sample Tractor beverages from six juice taps and four bubblers serving iced tea and lemonade. De Babel will also offer dairy-free tahini ice cream as part of its expanded range of thoughtful alternatives. The same food, with a more expansive experience Despite the added retail and hospitality elements, the made-to-order menu remains at the center of De Babel. The new restaurant delivers the same Middle Eastern flavors associated with the original location while giving guests more ways to experience the brand – whether stopping for a quick meal, gathering on the patio or purchasing traditional products to take home. “This is not about changing the food or turning De Babel into something unfamiliar,” Kandeel said. “It is about protecting what our guests already love and building a better experience around it.” A quiet and intentional opening De Babel will not hold a traditional grand-opening celebration or introduce promotional discounts. Instead, the restaurant will open quietly and intentionally. The measured opening period will allow the team to strengthen its systems, build consistency under pressure and refine the guest experience before Metro Phoenix enters its high season and welcomes the return of winter visitors. “We are choosing to grow with discipline,” Kandeel said. “Before the busiest season arrives, we want our team to become confident, consistent and fully prepared to deliver outstanding hospitality every day.” The post Middle Eastern Concept De Babel Opens Second Scottsdale, Arizona appeared first on QSR Magazine .

articles.title: O’Charley’s Abruptly Shutters All Company-Owned Locations
articles.titleKo: O’Charley’s Abruptly Shutters All Company-Owned Locations
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . O'Charley's was founded in 1971. O’Charley’s has shuttered company-owned restaurants across the country, bringing the once-prominent casual-dining chain closer to disappearing after years of contraction. Employees at multiple restaurants said Wednesday would be their final day, with many locations scheduled to close permanently at 8 p.m. The shutdown came with little warning for workers and without a public explanation from the Nashville-based company. In O’Charley’s home market, Nashville television station WKRN contacted managers at six of the chain’s eight Middle Tennessee restaurants. They said employees at all eight had been informed that their restaurants would close Wednesday at 8 p.m. The company did not respond to the station’s repeated requests for comment. NewsChannel 5 in Nashville reported that employees at multiple restaurants were informed Tuesday that Wednesday would be their last day. The Manchester Times in Manchester, Tennessee , separately spoke with a staff member who said employees received only one day’s notice. The restaurant had operated in the community for nearly 20 years. In Marion, Illinois, the restaurant’s general manager told local television station KFVS that the O’Charley’s would permanently close at 8 p.m. Wednesday. Employees there were informed of the decision Wednesday morning. The restaurant had been part of the Marion community for 24 years. In Kentucky, a staff member at the Hopkinsville restaurant confirmed to local radio station WHOP that the location would permanently close Wednesday at 8 p.m. The employee said nearly all O’Charley’s restaurants were expected to shut down. The two O’Charley’s restaurants in Northern Kentucky, located in Florence and Cold Spring, were also closing. The closures did not immediately include every restaurant. The franchised O’Charley’s in Niles, Ohio, will remain open until September 27 before permanently closing, according to an employee who spoke with the Columbus Dispatch . O’Charley’s Facebook and Instagram accounts were deactivated Wednesday, according to several local outlets. Its website, however, remained operational as of Wednesday evening. At its peak, O’Charley’s grew to nearly 250 restaurants across the U.S. The chain reported 244 locations across 19 states in 2010, including 234 company-owned restaurants and 10 franchised units. Charlie Watkins founded O’Charley’s in 1971 on 21st Avenue near Vanderbilt University in Nashville. The concept is now majority owned by Cannae Holdings. On September 9, JOE & THE JUICE is rolling out a new menu and a global campaign to own the morning. The chain is refreshing and expanding its morning line-up – coffee, functional smoothies and shots, bowls, plus a new hot breakfast menu featuring eggs – bringing it together for the first time as one coordinated push. JOE has sold its iconic juices, coffee and morning products for years, and the name itself is slang for coffee. Yet despite guests already starting their day with JOE, survey data shows that one in four people still don’t think of JOE as a morning destination – a gap the new menu and campaign are now set out to close. The new hot egg products will see their widest rollout in the UK and US, but will also be available in select stores across the Nordics, Europe and in several of JOE’s franchise markets, including the Middle East, while all markets are simultaneously sharpening their focus on the morning experience. “We’ve built our name on juice and coffee, made fresh, at lunch and in the afternoon. Mornings currently make up a smaller share of JOE’s business than lunch and afternoon, and the company sees it as one of the most overlooked growth opportunities. Emphasis will vary by market, but the ambition is the same everywhere: making JOE the natural first stop of the day. “We’ve offered a breakfast range for quite a while, but demand for eggs specifically has grown, and it gives our morning guests more to choose from. Jersey Mike's has over 1,600 restaurants in its pipeline. Jersey Mike’s has a clear destination for its restaurants. The sandwich giant wants average unit volumes to climb from roughly $1.4 million to $2 million. Its path there is starting with transactions. Same-store sales rose 2.3 percent in the second quarter, accelerating from 1.7 percent in Q1. The increase was driven primarily by transactions, and momentum carried into the third quarter, with comps tracking above 3 percent at the time of Jersey Mike’s inaugural earnings call on Wednesday. The company expects same-store sales growth of 2.5 to 3 percent for the full year, including 3 to 4 percent in the third quarter. Pricing is expected to contribute 1 percentage point or less during the second half. Jersey Mike’s made a deliberate decision in late 2025 to rely less on price and put more energy into traffic. “We made a conscious decision last year in the fourth quarter to reduce the amount of price we took as a brand and focus our efforts on growing transactions for the long term, which we believe is a much healthier way to grow the business,” CEO Charles Morrison said during the brand’s Q2 earnings call. Despite brand awareness of roughly 90 percent, the chain sees room to attract customers who know its name but visit infrequently, particularly Gen Z and Hispanic consumers. Digital marketing accounted for less than 1 percent of spending before climbing above 20 percent in the first half of 2026. Loyalty registrations increased 22 percent year-over-year, and ad awareness among Hispanic guests rose 6 percent. Morrison said Jersey Mike’s had done little call-to-action digital advertising before 2026. The shift gives the chain another tool to convert recognition into visits and eventually move customers into its loyalty ecosystem. The opportunity is substantial. Jersey Mike’s has an estimated 12 million to 13 million loyalty users, including roughly 7 million active members. Those active customers visit approximately once per month. Morrison believes the database can eventually reach 30 million to 50 million users. Digital sales also increased roughly 200 basis points during Q2 and accounted for 43 percent of sales. Jersey Mike’s sees that figure eventually reaching 60 to 70 percent. Delivery represents just under 20 percent of total sales, but first-party delivery accounts for only roughly 3 percent. The company sees first-party delivery eventually reaching 10 percent of sales as more guests order through Jersey Mike’s own digital channels. “We’ve seen that segment grow this year, but it’s from a very low base. But we do know that our marketing efforts are working to drive more customers to that channel and present them with a better value proposition, notably our loyalty program,” Morrison said. Scott Murphy, president of Dunkin’ and chief brand officer of Inspire, will serve as interim CEO. The Journal reported that Murphy told employees he does not expect Inspire’s strategy or direction to change during Brown’s absence. Inspire also expressed confidence that Brown will return after his recovery. The timing comes during a pivotal stretch for one of the world’s largest restaurant companies. In May, Inspire confidentially submitted a draft registration statement with the SEC for a proposed IPO. The Journal previously reported that an IPO could arrive by the end of 2026, although the process could extend into early 2027. Brown became CEO of Arby’s in 2013 and helped oversee the chain’s turnaround before Arby’s Restaurant Group acquired Buffalo Wild Wings for $2.9 billion in 2018. That deal led to the formation of Inspire. The company quickly grew through a string of major acquisitions. Sonic joined the portfolio in 2018 in a deal valued at roughly $2.3 billion, followed by Jimmy John’s in 2019. Inspire then acquired Dunkin’ Brands in 2020 for $11.3 billion, bringing Dunkin’ and Baskin-Robbins into the fold in one of the largest restaurant transactions in industry history. Today, Inspire oversees more than 33,400 restaurants across Dunkin’, Buffalo Wild Wings, Buffalo Wild Wings GO, Arby’s, Jimmy John’s, Sonic, and Baskin-Robbins. The brands combined for $33.4 billion in global system sales in 2025 and are supported by roughly 650,000 company and franchise employees. Inspire is controlled by private equity firm Roark Capital. Murphy brings extensive experience inside the portfolio to the interim CEO position. He has spent more than two decades with Dunkin’ and its predecessor organization, holding positions that included COO of Dunkin’ and president of Dunkin’ Americas before becoming brand president. He was named Inspire’s chief brand officer in 2023. Several of Inspire’s concepts also have histories as public companies. Sonic traded publicly for roughly 27 years before Inspire acquired it, Buffalo Wild Wings spent about 15 years on the public markets, and Dunkin’ Brands was public for nearly a decade before its acquisition. articles.title: The ‘Burger Revolution’ Arrives at Carl’s Jr.
articles.titleKo: The ‘Burger Revolution’ Arrives at Carl’s Jr.
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Carl's Jr. is launching the Angus Maximus to introduce customers to its new cooked-to-order standard. There are a few layers to how Carl’s Jr. plans to talk about one of the most impactful brand changes in some time. But chain president Iwona Alter returns to the obvious. “All in all,” says Alter, a former Habit Burger COO who joined in January, “we call this whole program a ‘Burger Revolution,’ because that’s what it is. We are changing how we are making our burgers.” Naturally, this represents a consequential turn for a brand founded 85 years ago as a hot dog cart (a drive-in model opened four years later in Anaheim, California, with the “Jr.” version arriving in 1956 as a smaller, faster unit). Burgers have been on the menu dating to 1946—the official start of the “Baby Boom” generation. How Carl’s Jr. plans to ignite a “burger revolution” harkens back as well. It’s ditching pre-cooked patties, stepping away from hot-holding stations (Prince Castle), and cooking every burger to order. When Alter was appointed brand president, she brought two-plus decades of burger experience to the title, having spent 13 years at Jack in Box, including two as CMO, before her tenure at Habit. She says Carl’s Jr’s began having conversations under new leadership. The brand’s parent company, CKE Restaurants (along with Hardee’s), tapped Joe Guith as CEO in March 2025, coming over from Church’s Texas Chicken and prior stops at GoTo Foods, McAlister’s Deli, Cinnabon, and Coca-Cola. He was CKE’s third CEO since 2023, following Ned Lyerly and Max Wetzel, the latter of which now directs Tropical Smoothie Café. As is often the case with any redirect of this scope, Alter says, Carl’s Jr. looked at how it could get back to the core of who it was as a brand. That’s felt different over the decades, she says, but one recurring thread was “being bold,” whether it’s flavor, branding, or design. Secondly, though, how do you progress that into the present? “And think of how that boldness looks like?” she says. Carl’s Jr. turned to social listening and survey tools to ask guests. The most-common response wasn’t a complex dilemma: customers wanted hot burgers, consistently. When done correctly, Carl’s Jr.’s char-broiled equity proved clear and its product held ground in the most-crowded QSR field there is. Carl’s Jr. ended 2025 with 992 stores and average-unit volumes of $1.422 million, good for 13 th among the 14 burger brands in this year’s QSR 50 by systemwide sales ($1.425 billion ). Ahead of Carl’s Jr. was Shake Shack ($1.541 billion) and behind, Freddy’s ($1.04 billion). So, what was the path to consistency? There weren’t going to be any shortcuts, Alter says. Carl’s Jr. needed to transform the entire near-1,000-unit system regarding how it delivered a hot patty. While the idea wasn’t convoluted (cook to order), it did present a material shift in production, execution, and mindset. One note, Alter explains, is Carl’s Jr. was already here on other pieces. Stores chop lettuce and slice tomatoes and onions in-restaurant every day. “So, why not the patty?” Alter says. “And knowing the guests are looking for that. Knowing that yeah, the dollar now has to work so much harder because as I’m spending it, I want something that will satisfy the craving.” As Carl’s Jr. explored its brand premise, a mantra kept emerging: “Nobody craves a compromise.” Although processes and equipment factored in, employees were the ones tasked with embracing that and making it happen, Alter says. Carl’s Jr. started by explaining internally why it was pushing toward cooked-to order. Pilots ran late last year and Carl’s Jr. polled team members on their personal takes. Would they want this if they walked in? Then, Carl’s Jr.’s restaurant excellence team devised how back-of-house efforts would change in light of answering the question. articles.title: Speed Wins: The Restaurants That Hire First Are Winning the Talent Race
articles.titleKo: Speed Wins: The Restaurants That Hire First Are Winning the Talent Race
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . An unfilled restaurant position impacts far more than recruiting. For years, restaurant hiring has been treated like a numbers game. Post a job, collect applications, review resumes, schedule interviews, and hope the best candidate is still available when you’re ready to make a decision. Today’s hiring market doesn’t work that way. One of the biggest competitive advantages in restaurant hiring isn’t offering the highest wage or the biggest signing bonus. Increasingly, it’s speed. Great candidates have options, and the restaurant that reaches them first often has the best opportunity to hire them. Great Candidates Don’t Stay on the Market Hourly workers aren’t necessarily spending weeks evaluating opportunities. Many are applying to multiple restaurants at the same time, often directly from their phones and sometimes within minutes of each other. The first employer to acknowledge an application, answer questions, and invite a qualified candidate to an interview immediately stands out. By the time another restaurant reviews applications two or three days later, that same candidate may already have an interview scheduled or have accepted another position. Hiring delays don’t just cost time. They cost talent. Think about two restaurants hiring for the exact same position. The first reviews applications every few days. A manager manually contacts candidates, waits for responses, and goes back and forth trying to schedule interviews. The second responds almost immediately. The candidate gets their questions answered, selects an interview time, and could be sitting across from a manager the following day. Both restaurants might offer similar compensation, culture, and opportunities. The difference is that one created momentum while the candidate was still interested. That’s the advantage of speed. The Cost of Waiting An unfilled restaurant position impacts far more than recruiting. When a restaurant is short staffed, managers spend more time covering shifts, existing employees take on additional responsibilities, and guest service can suffer. Over time, that added pressure can contribute to burnout and even more turnover. This creates a cycle restaurant operators know all too well. You’re short staffed, so your existing team works harder. Your team becomes frustrated, which can lead to more turnover. Suddenly, you’re not trying to fill one position anymore. Every additional day a critical role remains vacant has a cost, which is why reducing the time between application and interview matters so much. Candidates Expect Faster Communication Today’s candidates are accustomed to getting immediate responses in nearly every part of their lives. They can order dinner, book a ride, make a reservation, or schedule an appointment from their phone in minutes. Those expectations are carrying over into hiring. When applicants don’t hear back quickly, many aren’t going to wait. They’re going to keep applying elsewhere. At Swob, we’ve built our platform around this idea. Instant candidate communication, automated interview scheduling, and real time notifications are designed to help restaurant operators engage qualified candidates while their interest is at its highest. Instead of allowing applications to sit untouched for days, technology can help operators move candidates from application to conversation to interview much faster. This doesn’t mean removing the human side of hiring. In fact, I believe it’s the opposite. Technology should remove the administrative work that prevents those human conversations from happening sooner. That’s particularly important in restaurants. articles.title: How Top Growing Franchise Brands Have Cracked the Code on Real Estate Development

One way a franchisor can make a healthy impact on new franchisees is by investing in an incentive structure. For aspiring entrepreneurs, it almost feels like there’s an artform to mastering the delicate balance between ambition and risk. In today’s economy, achieving that harmony takes more skill than before as costs rise, and available real estate grows scarce. The path to opening a single profitable franchise location now calls for sharper strategy and data-backed decision-making. For many first-time franchisees, real estate has become one of the biggest obstacles to work through on the way to a grand opening. With the high-risk environment not changing anytime soon, the franchisors best positioned for growth are the ones rethinking how they can best tackle the real estate process for their prospective franchisees. Franchisor and Franchisee Real Estate Relationship When brands rapidly expand, a disconnect can form between franchisee and franchisor during the site-search process, especially as costs climb. Franchisors need to prioritize the relationship with the franchisee prospect by walking them through the brand’s support from day one. Be transparent about what site selection fully entails: data, realistic timelines, and the costs franchisees should expect to encounter in the market they are looking to expand in. For franchisees to succeed, franchisors must stay actively involved when evaluating potential sites. Franchisees are better equipped to make confident decisions when they understand what they’re walking into. Reviewing demographic data, traffic patterns and competitive density helps prevent costly missteps for franchisees before they happen. Having the real estate expertise to notice when a site that looks promising on paper is the wrong fit in reality will benefit franchisees who are new to the industry. Franchisors that invest that time up front see stronger, longer-lasting partnerships as a result. The shift to shared responsibility is an encouraging development for franchising. It suggests that the industry is maturing into a model that values the strength of both the franchisor and franchisee and does not prioritize one over the other. Benefits of Franchisee Incentives One way a franchisor can make a healthy impact on new franchisees is by investing in an incentive structure. Franchisors can’t change interest rates or construction costs, but they can offer equipment packages, phased royalties, and franchise fee incentives to relieve some of that pressure. Done well, these incentives can lower the bar for entry and create greater confidence for aspiring franchisees. Nontraditional Growth With traditional real estate scarce and expensive, more brands are buying into the idea of nontraditional formats like travel plazas, college campuses, or shared spaces that reduce the real estate burden altogether. These locations often come with lower buildout costs, smaller footprints, and a built-in customer base from the existing vendors. For brands open to nontraditional expansion, there’s an opportunity to succeed in markets where a standalone location would be difficult to justify. These formats will never replace traditional development, but they are giving brands additional paths to scale. The brands succeeding with this approach aren’t treating nontraditional locations as a fallback, but are evaluating each opportunity with the same rigor as a traditional site. Used well, nontraditional locations are a complement to a brand’s portfolio rather than a compromise. articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Pura Vida Miami , the all-day café and lifestyle brand operating 55 locations across six states and Washington D.C., today announced the appointment of Donnie Upshaw as Chief People and Culture Officer . Upshaw joins Co-Founders Omer and Jennifer Horev and the company’s expanding executive leadership team as Pura Vida Miami continues its national expansion. As the company enters its next chapter, Pura Vida is investing not only in new cafés and markets, but in the people, leadership and culture required to build an enduring organization. In his role, Upshaw will lead Pura Vida’s people and culture strategy, with responsibility for attracting and developing exceptional talent, strengthening leadership at every level of the organization, improving employee engagement and retention, and building the systems and infrastructure necessary to support the company as it scales. “As we build the next chapter of Pura Vida, one of my greatest responsibilities as CEO is to make sure we are not simply building a bigger company – we are building a better one,” said Omer Horev, Co-Founder and CEO of Pura Vida Miami. “I believe the strongest companies are built by people who genuinely care – about the guest, about their teammates, about the details, and about what we are building together. Donnie brings a deep understanding of what it takes to build strong teams, develop great leaders and create an environment where people can grow with the company. I think about our organization much like a great sports team,” Horev continued. “We may play different positions and have different responsibilities, but we wear the same jersey and are working toward the same goal. Bringing Donnie into our leadership team is an important investment in the company and culture we intend to build in the longterm.” Donnie Upshaw, Chief People and Culture Officer Upshaw joins Pura Vida Miami following an eight-year tenure with Wingstop, where he held senior leadership roles across people, brand and restaurant operations during a period of significant growth and transformation. He brings expertise spanning leadership development, succession planning, talent acquisition, workforce strategy and organizational effectiveness. At Pura Vida, Upshaw will work closely with executive leadership to strengthen leadership capabilities, develop talent from within and create opportunities for employees to grow into management and leadership roles. Central to his role will be preserving the entrepreneurial culture, hospitality and sense of community that have distinguished the brand as it scales. “Pura Vida Miami has built something truly special—a brand with an incredible culture, passionate people and an ambitious vision for the future,” said Donnie Upshaw, Chief People and Culture Officer of Pura Vida Miami. “I’m excited to help build the leadership, talent and capabilities to support our growth while maintaining the culture and sense of community that makes Pura Vida so special. I want Pura Vida to be a place where exceptional people want to build their careers and where leaders are developed from within.” Upshaw’s appointment further strengthens Pura Vida Miami’s senior leadership team as the company continues to invest in the people, operational capabilities and infrastructure needed to support its national expansion. His appointment follows the company’s recent additions of Andrew McCaughan as Chief Development Officer, Chad Brauze as Chief Culinary Officer, and Bruno Cardinali as Chief Marketing Officer in June 2026. Over the past nine months alone, TGI Fridays has accelerated its international expansion by signing new development agreements in Kenya and the Maldives, while extending strategic partnerships to drive continued growth across Peru, Japan, Mexico, the Philippines, Greece, Cyprus and Spain. Collectively, these agreements have added more than 150 restaurants to the brand’s global development pipeline, reinforcing the strength of TGI Fridays’ international franchise network and demonstrating the continued global demand for one of the world’s most iconic casual dining brands. articles.title: Five Guys is Bringing its Word-of-Mouth Formula into the Digital Age
articles.titleKo: Five Guys is Bringing its Word-of-Mouth Formula into the Digital Age
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Five Guys is one of the largest burger chains in the U.S. Five Guys built a restaurant empire without many of the tools that have become standard across the industry. The fast casual is the 10th-largest burger chain in America in terms of systemwide sales; it earned $2.3 billion in 2025. In terms of unit count, it is the seventh-largest, ending last year with 1,511 U.S. restaurants. There is no loyalty program. The menu has stayed remarkably focused. Marketing has never relied on a constant stream of limited-time products. For decades, much of the brand’s reputation traveled through customers telling other customers where to find a good burger and fries. Forty years after Five Guys opened its first restaurant, that foundation isn’t being discarded. But the way people discover restaurants, order food, and communicate with brands has changed enough for Five Guys to rethink how it tells its story. That work is now part of the job for chief commercial officer Navin Sharma, whose responsibilities span marketing, digital, loyalty, e-commerce, analytics and consumer insights. The position gives Five Guys a dedicated commercial operation at a time when the chain continues to add restaurants and sees an opportunity to introduce more consumers to what happens behind the counter. “One of the big drivers of success for the brand historically has changed in today’s environment and that’s the word of mouth aspect of it,” Sharma says. The restaurant walls offer a clue to how Five Guys originally built its reputation. Reviews from newspapers and magazines have long been part of the décor, showcasing outside validation of the food and experience. Much of that conversation now happens through social media, where Five Guys sees an opening to tell stories that consumers may have never heard. Fresh-cut fries are one example. Five Guys makes them from fresh potatoes inside its restaurants, a process Sharma gained a new appreciation for when he trained in a store after joining the company. “There’s a lot of things like that we do that people don’t know,” Sharma says. “So there’s a lot of stories we can share.” The challenge is building a more sophisticated commercial engine without stripping away the simplicity that helped Five Guys grow. Sharma doesn’t see the assignment as a reinvention. He wants new marketing and digital capabilities to serve as an extension of what Five Guys already does. That applies to menu innovation, too. Five Guys isn’t preparing to chase every product trend or stretch into categories far removed from burgers, fries and shakes. “You won’t see us do a chicken sandwich or anything like that,” Sharma says. “It’s still going to be burgers and fries and shakes. We might do a slightly different version of a burger perhaps, or a different version of the shake, but it’ll still be those core items that people love.” One untapped source of innovation already exists inside the menu. Customers can create a huge number of burger and shake combinations from Five Guys’ existing ingredients, giving the chain material it can surface through digital channels without expanding far outside its core. Sharma sees potential to showcase combinations created by employees and customers, introducing guests to orders they may not have considered on their own. Loyalty could eventually become another vehicle for those discoveries. Five Guys is working on a loyalty program after hearing requests for one from customers. Sharma says frequency and customer data are useful benefits, but the initial motivation is rewarding the chain’s most frequent guests. articles.title: Hilton Ramps up Growth Across Ireland with DoubleTree by Hilton Ashbourne Signing
articles.titleKo: Hilton Ramps up Growth Across Ireland with DoubleTree by Hilton Ashbourne Signing
articles.originalSummary: Hilton is expanding its presence in Ireland with a range of signings, openings and brand debuts, marking a significant step in its growth and building on its existing portfolio of eight hotels across six brands. The upcoming openings will create more than 150 jobs and will bring the number of team members working at Hilton hotels in Ireland to nearly 1,000. The growth is boosted by an agreement to bring DoubleTree by Hilton to Ireland with the conversion of a 156-room hotel in Ashbourne, near Dublin. Expected to open as DoubleTree by Hilton Ashbourne in early 2027 , the hotel will undergo a comprehensive refurbishment, including upgrades to guest rooms, public spaces, restaurants and bars. Located 25 minutes from Dublin Airport, the property is well placed for business and leisure demand, further strengthening Hilton’s presence in Greater Dublin. Richard Mc Dermott, proprietor of DoubleTree by Hilton Ashbourne, said: “Partnering with Hilton marks an exciting next step for the hotel. Alongside a refreshed guest experience, it will help create employment opportunities and deliver long-term value for the local area. Backed by Hilton’s commercial strength and global loyalty programme, we’re confident the hotel will become a go-to destination for guests visiting Dublin and beyond.” The signing follows the opening of Home2 Suites by Hilton Dublin City Centre , marking the brand’s European debut. The 290-suite property introduces Hilton’s fast-growing extended-stay concept to the region, offering apartment-style accommodation designed for both short and longer stays. Located just moments from O’Connell Street, the hotel caters to the growing demand for flexible, home-like accommodation among both business and leisure travellers. Paul Blackmore, vice president, development, UK & Ireland, Hilton, said: “Ireland’s enduring appeal makes it an attractive market for Hilton, with strong demand in cities and across the regions. The opening of Home2 Suites, alongside new signings including DoubleTree by Hilton Ashbourne, and continued expansion of brands such as Tapestry Collection by Hilton, underlines our confidence in the country. We remain focused on expanding our footprint and working with owners and partners to bring the right brands to the right locations while supporting tourism and long-term investment.” Alongside these developments, Hilton recently signed Cork City Centre, Tapestry Collection by Hilton . Expected to open in 2027 in partnership with JMK Group, the 103-room hotel will be located on South Terrace in the heart of Cork and will feature a mix of standard guestrooms and extended-stay accommodation, alongside a restaurant, bar and fitness facilities. The signing marks Hilton’s debut in Cork and builds on the growth of its lifestyle portfolio across the UK and Ireland. Hilton is also expanding its presence across Northern Ireland with a number of landmark projects spanning multiple brands. In Portrush, Hilton celebrated the one-year anniversary since the opening of The Marcus Portrush, Tapestry Collection by Hilton , which marked the brand debut of Tapestry Collection in Northern Ireland. It also expanded its DoubleTree portfolio through the signings of DoubleTree by Hilton Belfast City Ten Square and DoubleTree by Hilton Derry ‑ Londonderry. Looking ahead, Hilton is set to debut another brand in Northern Ireland – Tempo by Hilton Belfast City Centre . Expected to be the first Tempo by Hilton opening outside of the United States, the 144-room lifestyle hotel will bring Hilton’s wellness-focused brand to international markets for the first time, representing a significant milestone in the brand’s global growth strategy.

articles.originalSummary: Ever fancied a Highland cow in your bathroom? Or perhaps a preening peacock, a glorious lion, or a giraffe with serious design attitude? Now you can. Kinedo has expanded its Kinewall range with a new portfolio of animal-inspired wall panel designs under its Signature collection. The new Highland Cow, Peacock and Lion panels join the distinctive Giraffe design launched last year, creating a bold new line-up for homeowners and designers looking to bring real personality into the bathroom. articles.title: Angelo Cappellini & Opera Contemporary and the Villa Jolanda project in Brunate on Lake Como
articles.titleKo: Angelo Cappellini & Opera Contemporary and the Villa Jolanda project in Brunate on Lake Como
articles.originalSummary: Set on the hills of Brunate overlooking the breathtaking panorama of Lake Como, Villa Jolanda becomes the stage for an interior design project that celebrates the excellence of Italian design and craftsmanship through the intervention of Angelo Cappellini and Opera Contemporary , created in collaboration with Garamonds. Nestled within an architecturally charming setting, the villa has been reinterpreted through an interior design project capable of enhancing its historical identity with an elegant, sophisticated language perfectly in harmony with the atmosphere of the location. Taking center stage in the project are furnishings by Opera Contemporary and Angelo Cappellini, carefully selected to create a harmonious dialogue between historical heritage and contemporary sensibility. The rooms of the residence feature a refined selection of Clarissa, Osiride, and Ivette beds by Opera Contemporary, complemented by furnishings distinguished by soft lines, fine materials, and delicate beige and natural tones. The interiors blend seamlessly into the villa’s original spaces, helping to shape intimate and relaxing environments designed to offer an exclusive and contemporary hospitality experience. The designer beds by Opera Contemporary express a welcoming, warm, and sensual aesthetic, achieved through the use of fine materials, artisanal craftsmanship, and a rich variety of textures that enhance the feeling of comfort and intimacy. The color palettes, dominated by natural tones with occasional accents of color, define refined and contemporary environments in which the bed becomes the absolute centerpiece of the bedroom space. The bedroom, the most personal space in the home, thus transforms into a private retreat away from daily stress: a place dedicated to relaxation, wellbeing, and the restoration of one’s energy. A distinctive element of the project is also the wooden dependency separated from the main villa, conceived as an elegant space dedicated to the traditional “five o’clock tea.” Angelo Cappellini interprets the charm of great Italian decorative tradition through a Louis XV-style living room composed of sofas, armchairs, chairs, and coffee tables with crystal tops. The artisanal craftsmanship, carved details, and fine finishes fully express the brand’s savoir-faire, creating an environment with a refined and timeless character. The intervention at Villa Jolanda highlights the ability of Angelo Cappellini and Opera Contemporary to design environments where aesthetics, comfort, and identity coexist in perfect balance. It is a project that interprets contemporary luxury through manufacturing quality, stylistic research, and the enhancement of Italian heritage, set in one of the most iconic and internationally renowned destinations of the Lake Como area. The collaboration with Garamonds arose naturally, driven by a shared vision of hospitality and the authentic value of Italian lifestyle. Villa Jolanda represents a place capable of attracting an international clientele seeking not only an exclusive destination, but an experience deeply rooted in tradition, elegance, and a culture of beauty. From the very early stages of the project, a strong synergy emerged among the companies involved, united by the desire to enhance the historic character of the villa through furnishings and atmospheres capable of expressing Italian craftsmanship. This is a language made of artisanal details, refined materials, and high-end manufacturing techniques, designed for an international audience that recognizes Italy as a global benchmark for style and quality. In this context, the collaboration between Angelo Cappellini, Opera Contemporary, and Garamonds has helped create environments that are fully consistent with the soul of the villa, where contemporary design and classical tradition coexist in perfect balance, offering guests a sophisticated and timeless experience.

articles.title: Putting on the Ritz: Manchester Hoteliers Association Celebrates 21st Anniversary with ‘Roaring 20s’ Ball
articles.titleKo: Putting on the Ritz: Manchester Hoteliers Association Celebrates 21st Anniversary with ‘Roaring 20s’ Ball
articles.originalSummary: Membership organisation comprising more than 75 of Greater Manchester’s key hotels, the MHA, has announced plans for its 21st annual ball. The popular event is hosted every year to raise money for local charities and celebrate the hospitality industry. Taking place on Thursday 29th October, the ball will return to Emirates Old Trafford for the second year running. Since the organisation’s inception, one of its key pillars has been charitable donations, raising hundreds of thousands of pounds from the annual celebration over two decades. This year’s chosen charities are Barnabus, Greater Manchester Mayor’s Charity, Wood Street Mission and national charity, Hospitality Action. MHA chair, Matt Townley, has set lofty aims to beat last year’s £45,000 raised. The event, which will take a ‘Roaring 20s’ theme, will also play host to the MHA’s annual awards, voted for by a panel of business and industry experts. Following usual proceedings, there will be a total of nine trophies presented on the night, including Unsung Hero, Rising Star, and Outstanding Contribution to Hospitality. Matt, who is also Group Operations Director at Dakota Hotels, said : “Now in its 21st year, the MHA ball has become a cherished tradition within our industry, providing an opportunity to recognise achievements and support important charitable causes. “Manchester’s hotel and hospitality community continues to demonstrate remarkable resilience and collaboration, and this year’s event will be a fitting celebration of those qualities. We look forward to welcoming colleagues, partners, and friends from across the sector for what promises to be a memorable evening as always.” The event has also amassed support from key local and national sponsors such as, WGC, Expedia, MMU, Stephenson’s, Elix Air, and Percipient. MHA’s five key industry partners; Nespresso, Silentnight, Howden, Mint People, and Purple Story will also continue supporting the organisation for a second year running. Pamela Reckert at Manchester Metropolitan University, said : “Manchester Metropolitan University is proud to sponsor the 21st Manchester Hoteliers Association Ball and support an event that celebrates the people and achievements that make Greater Manchester’s hospitality industry so exceptional.” The ball will be taking place on Thursday 29th October at Emirates Old Trafford, with more than 800 people expected to turn out. Tickets are available and can be purchased here. Entries are now open for the MHA awards and can be submitted here.

At the heart of Musaafer's menu are select ingredients and spice blends, specifically sourced from families in India who have been using them for generations. Mithu Malik’s restaurant Musaafer—Urdu for “traveler”—takes its patrons on an unfiltered journey through India, inspired by executive chef Mayank Istwal’s 100-day journey through India’s states and territories. Along the way, Istwal didn’t just collect recipes—he cooked them in the very homes where they’d been passed down for generations, learning from cooks whose families had made these dishes long before him. When Malik opened this restaurant alongside her husband in Houston, it quickly earned recognition as the first Indian restaurant with a female owner in Texas to earn a Michelin star. Following the success of the Houston location, they opened another in New York City. At the heart of Musaafer’s menu, interwoven with the stories and faces of those Istwal met on his cultural trek through India, are the select ingredients and spice blends, specifically sourced from families in India who have been using them for generations. “Musaafer seeks to elevate Indian cuisine and take it away from the general concept of a big bowl of curry and rice with naan. Istwal’s journey is integral to our menu design, which rotates three times a year, because we’re constantly taking from the bank of recipes we built and brainstorming how to use modern techniques and artistic presentations,” Malik says. Take the laal maas, for example: a smoked goat meat dish smothered in mathania chili, freeze-dried garlic, and millet brittle. It hails from the northwestern state of Rajasthan, where chefs once accompanied kings on hunts into the jungle. The dish was traditionally made from game meat, but after hunting was banned in the 1970s, it’s now made from goats. Then there’s the masala papad appetizer, a modern interpretation of matthi, a deep-fried pastry traditionally eaten with pickled mango, also known as achar. Musaafer’s version is slightly thinner and crispier, with spice-cured tuna, avocado, and an achar emulsion. This is just the beginning of elevated Indian cuisine’s representation in the United States. Malik sees a bright future ahead—not just for Musaafer, but for a culture ready to experience the breadth and magic of Indian cuisine. For Eunji Lee, a South Korean pastry chef classically trained in Paris, it was a dream come true to combine her French training with Korean ingredients as executive pastry chef of Jungsik, the three-Michelin-star modern Korean restaurant in New York—and the first Korean restaurant in the U.S. to earn that distinction. Today, she owns her own pastry boutique in New York City, Lysée, whose menu combines three cultures—French, Korean, and the city itself. There’s the traditional Korean influence, like the matcha floating island dessert with Uji matcha and Yuja sorbet; the French, with madeleines made from passionfruit cream, passionfruit glaze and a roasted coconut crumble; and the classic New York marble pound cake, with a chocolate caramel glaze. Her favorite dessert reminds her of childhood—a cake made from Korean toasted brown rice mousse, caramel, pralines, and a pecan sable sourced from Georgia. The idea came to her from a childhood memory of her grandma, who lived in the countryside and farmed rice. She can remember the aroma of brown rice being cooked on the stove, and it sticks with her until this day. “I try to tell my story through my dishes, starting with the Korean ingredients and culture I grew up with, the French techniques that I learned, and who I am now, which is a New Yorker,” Lee says. “Dessert is its own language, and I want people to experience it in a deeper and more meaningful way.” Like Lee, Ochi Latjuba Vongerichten represents her dual culture through the New York City restaurants she owns with her husband and chef, C

articles.title: The Battle for the Bowl Heats Up in QSR
articles.titleKo: The Battle for the Bowl Heats Up in QSR
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . For Playa, standing out means building bowls around four things: taste, a “beneficial” ingredient story, visual appeal, and operational feasibility. Bowls have long been associated with health and nutrition, but the format now stretches far beyond its wellness-niche roots. From acai and smoothie bowls to salads, grains, and warm meals, bowl concepts are increasingly competing for everyday occasions—not just a post-workout snack or a light lunch. That shift shows up in consumer demand for portability, customization, recognizable ingredients, functional benefits, and food that still feels satisfying. For brands in the space, the opportunity is less about selling one definition of “healthy” than giving guests a flexible meal that fits their particular needs. An All-Day Occasion Juice It Up! has been selling acai bowls for more than two decades, back when the ingredient was unfamiliar enough that franchisees had to be taught how to pronounce it, says president and CEO Susan Taylor. The Southern California-based chain has watched the product move from a relatively small menu category into a much more central part of its business. Bowls historically have accounted for about 15 percent of the brand’s mix. Today, they are nearing 24 percent, Taylor says, with bowl mix up nearly 20 percent year over year. “It used to be something you’d see on the West Coast or Hawaii or in Florida,” Taylor says. “And then it’s just grown across the country.” Greater familiarity has helped. So has social media, which has made colorful, layered bowls more visible to younger consumers willing to explore new flavors and ingredients. But Taylor says the more meaningful shift is in how people are using bowls: not just as an occasional better-for-you treat, but as a meal that can fit throughout the day. Juice It Up! tracks four dayparts—breakfast, lunch, afternoon, and dinner—and Taylor says bowl sales have grown significantly in the morning and evening over the past two years. Some locations near gyms, for example, are seeing guests come in after workouts for a bowl. “It has legs to meet people where they’re at in how they want to eat during the day,” she says. The brand has responded by adding more options beyond a basic acai or dragon fruit base. Guests can choose from flavors such as coconut passion fruit and seasonal mango, layer in chia pudding or protein-infused yogurt, and build their own combinations. Texture, variety, and personalization are becoming bigger parts of the occasion. “Flavor and texture have become more of what I think the up-and-coming generations really look at when they’re looking at products,” Taylor says. The idea is to let bowls serve different needs—breakfast, an afternoon break, a meal replacement, or a way to add protein and fiber—without making guests choose between function and enjoyment. A Growing Category Gets More Competitive At Playa Bowls, the growth of the category has created a more segmented and competitive landscape. CMO Tim Hackbardt sees three broad buckets: classic acai shops, often independents or smaller chains; large smoothie brands that have added acai bowls; and bowl-first concepts like Playa, where smoothies are a secondary part of the business. “It’s been a very fast-growing category, at least for the past three years,” he says. “We’ve more than doubled in size ourselves.” That growth is likely to bring more competition, he adds, and eventually some separation between the brands that have a clear point of view and those that do not. Hackbardt expects the category to see some attrition over the next few years as the segment stabilizes around a core group of winners. articles.title: AI Can Launch the Campaign. Does It Know If Your Restaurant Needs One?
articles.titleKo: AI Can Launch the Campaign. Does It Know If Your Restaurant Needs One?
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Finding the problem and understanding what to do about it are two very different things. There’s been a change in the AI conversations I’m having with restaurant marketers. They’re no longer just asking how AI can help write copy or summarize a report. They’re bringing in sales and POS data (yes, sharing that data with an LLM raises its own questions, but that’s another conversation), looking for opportunities across their system, and asking AI what they should do next. And increasingly, AI can act on those recommendations. Meta has opened its ad platform through Model Context Protocol, or MCP, allowing tools like ChatGPT and Claude to work directly with ad accounts. Amazon has launched its own MCP server for advertisers, while Google is expanding its Ads MCP and agentic capabilities. For restaurant marketers, the implications are pretty significant. The distance between spotting a problem and doing something about it is getting much shorter. That’s exciting. But it also raises a more important question: Does AI have enough context to know what a restaurant actually needs? Imagine a 1,500-location QSR brand. Sales are down at 50 restaurants. An LLM can identify those locations in seconds. But what should happen next? One restaurant may need more local advertising. Another may have an offer that isn’t resonating. A third may be losing traffic because a competitor opened across the street. Another may have an operational problem that marketing won’t fix at all. Finding the problem and understanding what to do about it are two very different things. MCP makes it easier to execute the answer your LLM gives you. It doesn’t mean the LLM had the context to get that answer right. A Restaurant Is More Than Its Sales Data The obvious response might be to give the LLM more data. But that’s not really the problem. A large restaurant brand has national campaigns, regional programs and local marketing happening at the same time. Different budgets may be controlled by corporate, co-ops and franchisees. Certain offers may be available in one market but not another. Campaigns may already be running. And what worked at one group of restaurants may tell you something useful about what to try at another. All of that matters when deciding what a restaurant should do next. But some of the most important context may not exist in any system. The franchisee may know road construction has made the restaurant difficult to reach. A new competitor may have opened nearby. A school event could create an opportunity this weekend. Or the operator may know service times have slipped and spending more money to drive traffic right now would make the problem worse. That’s why the goal shouldn’t be to replace local knowledge with AI. It should be to combine what the operator knows with what the brand knows and what can be learned across the broader system. And the answer shouldn’t always be another ad campaign. Sometimes it’s paid media. Sometimes it’s organic social, direct mail or a different offer. Sometimes the best marketing decision is to do nothing until an operational issue gets fixed. Before AI Acts, Make Sure It Knows the Rules Once AI can actually take action, the stakes change. Whose budget is it spending? Is the offer approved for this restaurant? What’s already running? What has worked in similar situations? And is there local knowledge that could change the decision? For a restaurant brand with hundreds or thousands of locations, these aren’t edge cases. They’re everyday realities. If AI doesn’t have that context – along with the right rules and permissions – it probably isn’t ready to act on the recommendation. An audit trail matters, too. Promotions around specific products are a feature of many categories, but they tend to be especially pronounced in QSR marketing. Shouting out a limited or secret menu item is a specific job with multiple overlapping goals. You need the ad to put across the basic information that the product is out there. You need to tie it into your wider brand so people know where to get it and you need to do it in an entertaining, attention-grabbing way so the news doesn’t get lost in the media flow. This month we’re looking at how Wendy’s does all these things in just 15 seconds in their new ad for their Pretzel Bacon Pub Cheeseburger. With short-form (30 seconds or less) accounting for about 50 percent of all TV media , it’s amazing that Wendy’s could achieve this in just 15 seconds, as we’ve found that emotion needs time with the sweet spot being 20—40 seconds. System1’s Test Your Ad database shows longer ads tend to create more emotion because emotion builds over time. The burger is a relatively recent innovation, on menus from 2020 to 2022 and becoming a firm fan favorite. Earlier this year Wendy’s ran a “Bring It Back” bracket, where the Pretzel Bacon Pub Cheeseburger romped home in a fan vote. Customer demand for the burger is out there. Within two seconds, 77 percent of viewers know this is a Wendy’s ad according to System1’s Fast Fluency score. Rather than taking time away from the creative, this early brand recognition helps Wendy’s get more value from everything that follows. The ad calls the burger a “fan favorite”, introducing an element of social proof into the message, while showing a customer taking a bite reinforces its delicious (and crunchy) appeal. Because viewers already know who’s speaking, the entertainment works harder for the brand, ensuring the positive feelings generated by the ad are more likely to be attributed back to Wendy’s. With these basics established, the ad can get on with entertaining us. As he bites down, the customer is transported into a real pub, a fitting setting for this beer-sauce-enhanced burger (“It’s like a pub in a bun” says the voiceover). articles.originalSummary: UK spending on eating and drinking increased 1.8% year-on-year in August, according to the latest Barclays Consumer Spend report, with bars, pubs and clubs recording the strongest growth. Spending at bars, pubs and clubs rose 2.7% along with a 2.9% transaction growth, while spending at restaurants, cafes and bakeries increased 1.5% despite a 1.3% decline in transactions. Takeaway and fast-food spending was up 1.6% with a 1.3% growth in transactions.

articles.title: Tigermilk Brings Hacienda Grandeur to the Heart of East London
articles.titleKo: Tigermilk Brings Hacienda Grandeur to the Heart of East London
articles.originalSummary: Their modern South American inspired interior brings life to their largest site to dat e Following its successful opening in May, Tigermilk Spitalfields’s interior has emerged as one of the defining elements of the new flagship restaurant by Alexis and Nina Melikov, the group’s largest site to date. Designed by Studio Leche, Tigermilk’s in-house design studio, the space brings together hacienda-inspired architecture, layered materials and a warm, transportive atmosphere that has become central to the guest experience. Conceived as an escape in the heart of Spitalfields, the ambition was to build an environment that guests would immediately want to stay in, rather than one designed purely to be photographed. Central patios, generous proportions, fountains, handcrafted materials and lush greenery give the space its structure and soul, evoking the kind of environment that takes decades to settle into its surroundings. Antique furniture sits alongside bespoke pieces, and reclaimed terracotta, natural stone, marble and aged timber are used throughout, materials that carry history and wear it well. “People rarely talk about specific design features. They talk about the atmosphere,” adds Alexis. “If people leave believing the space possesses a history, then we have succeeded in creating something that feels authentic rather than constructed.” A considered selection of suppliers and craftspeople underpins the interior. Sogni and Pooky provide the lighting, Pierre Frey and Morris the fabrics and upholstery, and Mandarin Stone the marble and stone surfaces. Flexhouse – responsible for custom joinery, millwork and bespoke fabrication – also contributed to the furniture alongside vintage pieces and Leta, while Resources delivered the decorative wall finishes. Together they bring a layered quality to the space, as though each element has its own provenance and story. With its new 280-cover restaurant, hacienda-inspired interiors and striking luminescent bar stocked with more than 2700 bottles, Tigermilk Spitalfields invites guests into what feels like the brand’s thirteenth home. Through a considered interior scheme full of texture and attention to detail, the restaurant offers a transportive South American-inspired experience designed to engage every sense.

articles.title: Scooter’s Has a Role to Play in the Drive-Thru Coffee Rush
articles.titleKo: Scooter’s Has a Role to Play in the Drive-Thru Coffee Rush
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . As Dutch Bros and 7 Brew bid over sites, Black Rock Coffee Bar navigates publicly traded life , and Starbucks regains traction after years of choppiness , Scooter’s Coffee has steadily expanded in a category suddenly flush with growth brands. Scooter’s had 555 of its drive-thru-focused stores at the start of 2023. But that calendar proved a major catapult, with the company adding a net of 195 venues to exit at 650 (729 of which were franchised). Then, in 2024, Scooter’s grew by net 99 locations (96 franchised) and followed with development of 57 this past year, finishing at 906 (882 franchised and 24 affiliate run). It shouldn’t be long before the 1998-founded brand, which sprung up in Bellevue, Nebraska—the state’s oldest continuous settlement, dating back as a fur-trading post in the early 19 th Century—eclipses the 1,000-unit mark to join Dutch Bros (1,225 shops end of Q2), Starbucks (about 17,000 U.S.), and Dunkin’ ( roughly 10,000 ) as four-digit beverage brands. 7 Brew, at 800 or so today, is headed there, too, and should break through before the year turns over . Scooter’s likely will pass 1,000 sometime in 2027. According to its recent FDD, it’s planning 79 gross new franchised outlets across fiscal 2026 (and one company) and touts a pipeline of 242 agreements signed without a store opened yet. That includes 25 in Illinois, 22 in Florida, 20 in Texas, and double-digit deals inked in Georgia (11), Indiana (12), Michigan (11), Minnesota (15), and Missouri (11). This year’s growth webs out across a host of states, with a concentration of 12 planned for Illinois, seven in Indiana, and six apiece in Florida and Tennessee. That outline does not include potential closures. Scooter’s in 2025 opened 85 franchised restaurants, terminated two, had a non-renewal, and reacquired a location from a franchisee. Twenty-four Scooter’s ceased operations for “other reasons.” That number was 20 last year and two the year prior. Franchise openings have trended from 209 in 2023’s spurt (a year it sold 12 restaurants to franchisees) to 121 in 2024 and the noted 85 last calendar. Barring a material slide in trajectory, Scooter’s should be well within the 1,000-store orbit as 2027 comes into focus. As for how it compares by unit-level performance, Scooter’s finished 2025 with U.S. systemwide sales of $859 million and average-unit volumes just under $1 million. It marked the brand’s debut on the annual QSR 50 . CHECK OUT THE SNACK CATEGORY HERE Dutch Bros was at $2.2 billion systemwide sales and $2.1 million AUV, while 7 Brew reported $1.2 billion and $2.6 million, respectively. Starbucks was second only to McDonald’s overall in systemwide sales at $30.2 billion and generated AUVs hovering around $1.8 million. Dunkin’ hit $13.1 billion and $1.4 million. Black Rock, which had 181 restaurants year-end (it recently crossed 200 ) achieved $200 million on AUVs of $1.3 million . Scooter’s unravels an extensive Item 19 on its FDD. The brand reports results for “kiosk drive-thru stores” and franchised “end-cap drive-thrus.” On average, the kiosk definition applies to a location 650–700 square feet, while end-caps are 800–1,400. And to note regarding the term “kiosk,” this is what Scooter’s uses to illustrate a drive-thru-only standalone box that’s not attached to other real estate. There is generally no seating and sales primarily owe to drinks and associated food products through drive-up windows. They are located in parking lots near other retail shopping. End-caps are housed in strip centers with indoor ordering and a drive-thru window. The “other” moniker comprises restaurants in hospitals, malls, schools, airports, sporting venues, free-standing buildings, and sometimes includes “substantial” indoor seating with a drive-thru and public restrooms, or stores with only a site-specific service counter. articles.title: Bread Ahead launches owner-operator model with first UK bakery outside London
articles.titleKo: Bread Ahead launches owner-operator model with first UK bakery outside London
articles.originalSummary: Bakery brand Bread Ahead is launching an owner-operator model in Harpenden next month, marking the group’s first bakery in the UK outside its London heartland. The independent bakery and baking school will open on Harpenden High Street in a 2,500sq ft space combining a bakery, baking school and all-day dining venue. articles.title: After Difficult Year, Red Door Brands Sets Stage for Comeback
articles.titleKo: After Difficult Year, Red Door Brands Sets Stage for Comeback
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Number one on Kayla Edidin's to-do list is to bring in strong leadership and structure at the store level. It’s a Tuesday afternoon, and Kayla Edidin is sitting outside of an Arby’s in Texas. For the first time in years, she isn’t selling franchises; she owns them, as the new chief operating officer and majority partner of Red Door Brands with a 60 percent stake in the company and all its subsidiaries. Red Door Brands is a Knoxville-based, multi-brand portfolio company that operates nearly 20 franchised restaurants, including McAlister’s Deli, Little Caesars, Arby’s, and Main Squeeze Juice Co. across North and South Carolina, Georgia, and Texas. Edidin came on board in March 2026 to work alongside Argus Wiley, founder and CEO. For Edidin, the role represents a long-held wish being answered. After 20 years of operations experience as both a franchisor and franchisee, she moved into franchise development with Huddle House in 2018. She stayed on through Huddle House’s acquisition by Ascent Hospitality Management, which later also acquired Perkins Restaurant & Bakery, and went on to hold multiple roles leading franchise operations and development across the Ascent portfolio through 2025. “In my heart, I’m an entrepreneur, so this scratches an itch that’s been on my vision board forever. It’s been great to be connected to the soul of the restaurant again, the people who run it, and the communities we serve,” Edidin says. “I love the opportunities we’re going to create within Red Door Brands. I’ve had some exciting roles, but shifting into an equity role within the company is a lot more fulfilling than just selling franchises.” By all accounts, Edidin was leaving a rocket ship—Mike’s Red Tacos, where she’d sold more than 200 franchises for the emerging brand in its first year as vice president of franchise development. But she believed Red Door Brands could be one, too. 2025 was a difficult year for Red Door Brands. Matadoor Restaurant Group , a Red Door affiliate operating 22 Del Taco locations across Georgia and Alabama, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection amid mounting financial pressure. The filing has allowed Matadoor to continue operating while restructuring its finances, and Red Door has used the past year to streamline operations and refocus on long-term performance heading into 2026. Edidin represents a new era of stability for Red Door Brands, bringing a focus on operational excellence, system standardization, strategic expansion, and a goal to attract new capital partners and scale the portfolio to more than 100 units by 2028. Above all, she hopes to rebuild, little by little, trust and motivation among employees who’ve felt the impact of a hard year. She sees herself in them—this industry gave her opportunities she never would have had otherwise, like completing not just her undergrad but also an executive MBA program. “I’m big on mindset. It’s been a tough season for Red Door, but we’re going to be better than we were yesterday. They may have lost their way a little bit, but we’re going to elevate our standards and lean back on the core fundamentals that made us successful in the past,” Edidin says. “This is a breath of fresh air for the company. There’s less uncertainty around the future vision of how people can grow and build a life with us.” Edidin believes nobody becomes excellent on the easy path. Every aspect of Red Door Brands has been evaluated and refined, and that tough season has forced the company to ask the hard questions and pinpoint what it really needs to thrive. Number one on her to-do list is to bring in strong leadership and structure at the store level to guide and hold the team accountable in a positive way. The Flying Biscuit Café has signed a franchise agreement with Shreya Patel, who will bring the Atlanta-born breakfast and brunch brand to South Nashville. The agreement covers one café in the South Nashville Proper trade area, and site selection is underway. The address and opening date will be announced once a lease is signed. Patel brings a background in supply chain management along with restaurant ownership and management experience, and will serve as a full-time owner-operator, overseeing the café’s day-to-day operations. She was introduced to Flying Biscuit by business partners who came across the brand while operating restaurants in another market and stayed connected to it after relocating to Nashville. What sold her was the food and the operating model — a full breakfast and lunch business that closes in the afternoon, with no dinner or late-night shift to staff. South Nashville has seen steady residential growth and significant new investment in recent years, from GEODIS Park and the Nashville Fairgrounds to AJ Capital Partners’ 18-acre Wedgewood Village development and a 4,400-seat Live Nation venue opening this fall. Patel is aiming at a guest base of students, young professionals and area employees, with the Vanderbilt and Belmont campuses just beyond the neighborhood’s northwestern edge. The café will be the brand’s first in Nashville and its third in Tennessee, following Knoxville and Kingsport. “We chose Flying Biscuit because we wanted to bring a fun, welcoming brunch experience to the Nashville community, especially the vibrant area around Vanderbilt and the surrounding corporate community. We’re excited to create a place where students, professionals, families, and friends can come together over great food and make it their go-to neighborhood spot,” said Shreya Patel, franchise owner. When the café opens, guests can expect the menu Flying Biscuit is known for — all-day breakfast, shrimp and creamy dreamy grits, stuffed French toast, omelets, vegan scrambles, burgers and wraps — served from morning through the lunch hour. “Shreya and her team are targeting the South Nashville Proper trade area, which continues to show strong growth and aligns well with the brand’s daytime, community-focused model,” said Andrew Scherzer, partner and director of franchise development, Flying Biscuit Franchising. Beyond this first café, Patel hopes to grow to as many as three Flying Biscuit locations over time. Flying Biscuit Franchising continues to award territories across the Southeast and Texas. Prospective franchisees can review available markets and development requirements, and start a conversation with the development team, at flyingbiscuitfranchising.com. For menus, locations and ordering, visit flyingbiscuit.com. The menu features bold, Southern-inspired takes on brunch favorites — from stuffed French toast and famous shrimp and grits to hearty omelets, vegan scrambles, burgers and wraps. Many locations also offer a full bar with brunch-forward cocktails, including mimosa flights and the signature “Stage 5 Clinger” Bloody Mary. Flying Biscuit serves tens of thousands of biscuits every week and proudly provides full-service catering for events of all sizes. The brand is expanding through strategic franchise partnerships, with 43 locations open and 13 in development across Georgia, Alabama, Tennessee, South Carolina, North Carolina, Florida, Texas and Missouri — and more on the way. Leading the expansion is JHN Group, an Indiana-based restaurant and management company with previous restaurant operating experience in the Indianapolis market. Mr. Moto’s pizza dough is crafted over 48 hours to create a fluffy, airy border with a crispy bottom. The pizzeria offers a series of red pies (i.e. The Hulk with pepperoni, bacon, ham, sausage) and white pies (i.e. Smoky Greens with spinach, ricotta, garlic, sweet balsamic glaze). Twosome Place, South Korea’s leading premium café brand, announced its official entry into the U.S. with plans to open its first location in Alexandria, Virginia. The opening marks the next chapter in Twosome Place’s 25-year history and the first step in a broader U.S. growth strategy. Since opening its first café in Seoul in 2002, Twosome Place has grown to more than 1,750 locations, building a distinctive café experience around the pairing of specialty coffee and cake, where everyday moments become meaningful experiences. “Our debut in the Washington region is an important milestone for Twosome Place as we look ahead to future growth in the U.S.,” said Jay (Young Joo) Moon, CEO of Twosome Place Korea. “We’re excited to introduce American consumers to the café culture we’ve built over the past two decades, one centered on quality, hospitality, and creating a place where guests can gather over exceptional coffee and cake.” Located in Alexandria’s Old Town neighborhood, the first U.S. café will offer an assorted menu, featuring Twosome Place’s signature cakes, available both whole and by the slice, including the iconic Strawberry Chocolate Cream Cake, the only trademark-registered cake in Korea, with more than 3 million units sold annually, along with the bestselling Ice Box Cake, with more than 6 million sold annually. Alongside classic espresso beverages, Twosome Place will introduce Korean-inspired items developed specifically for the U.S. market, including handcrafted beverages like the Dalgona Cream Top, Black Sesame Latte, Misugaru Frappe—made with toasted multi-grains—and Korean Apple Cinnamon Tea, offering guests familiar formats with distinctive flavors. An all-day menu will feature K-Toast with Bulgogi and egg, K-Chicken Panini and Bibimbowl, making Twosome Place a destination throughout the day. The café is expected to open in mid-October. The Alexandria café will be located at 404 King Street, occupying approximately 2,604 square feet, featuring 78 seats including outdoor seating. More details regarding opening celebrations will be announced in the coming weeks. Additional U.S. locations are planned as Twosome Place continues its expansion, with two locations set to open soon. articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . The Build Your Own Burger ($13.25 single, $15.75 double) is a customizable adventure. Some people like their burgers simple. Others want to stack on the toppings, pile on the sauce and add a fried egg for good measure. Ruby Sunshine is bringing that anything-goes attitude to its seasonal menu, with savory dishes, early-fall sweets and new beverages available now at participating locations. The Build Your Own Burger ($13.25 single, $15.75 double) is a customizable adventure, starting with a single or double smash patty on a brioche bun. From there, guests can go classic with American or cheddar, or select toppings like pickled red onions, grilled portobello or fresh jalapeño, then finish with sauces ranging from remoulade and Creole mustard to apple cider-bourbon BBQ. For those who believe there’s no such thing as too much on a burger, add-ons include bacon, a fried egg, bacon-onion jam, chorizo, avocado and an extra patty. Guests looking for a lighter choice will enjoy the Kale Chicken Caesar ($18) featuring chopped kale, grilled chicken, parmesan, breadcrumbs, lemon and Caesar dressing. On the sweeter side, Ruby Sunshine is giving its beignets an early-fall makeover with Candied Apple Beignets ($7.25), served with candied apple compote, vanilla mascarpone and apple cider caramel. The drink menu shakes things up, too. The Apple Cider Mule ($10.50) combines vodka, apple compote, apple cider, ginger beer and lime, while the Whipped Strawberry Mimosa ($11.50) layers strawberry purée, lemon, coconut, sparkling wine and cold foam. “We got a little playful in the kitchen recently, challenging each other to give our guests some delicious combinations they might not expect from us,” said Chef Marla Chua, culinary director for Ruby Sunshine. “We wanted the burger to leave plenty of room for interpretation, whether you want to keep it simple or build an over-the-top masterpiece. That same sense of flexibility carries through the rest of our seasonal menu, with options for something lighter, something sweet or something to sip.” The early fall menu will be available at participating Ruby Sunshine locations from Sept. 2 through Sept. 29, while supplies last. For more information about Ruby Sunshine’s September menu and ongoing updates, visit rubybrunch.com or follow @BrunchWithRuby on Instagram, TikTok, X and Facebook.
