Firehouse Subs, the firefighter-founded hot sub brand known for its commitment to community impact, has officially opened its 200th restaurant in Canada. The landmark location in Calgary, Alberta marks a full-circle milestone: Alberta was home to the 100th Firehouse Subs Canadian restaurant, meaning the brand has doubled its national footprint since 2024. Franchisee Cody Gosling brought Firehouse Subs to Alberta with his first restaurant in Okotoks. This latest opening marks his sixth restaurant with the brand, a proud achievement for his family of multi-generational quick-service restaurant entrepreneurs. His continued growth with Firehouse Subs reflects the brand’s expanding presence across Canadian communities and its commitment to serving high-quality food while building meaningful connections rooted in community and public safety. “Okotoks is where it all started for us, so being part of restaurant number 200 feels incredibly special,” said Cody Gosling, Firehouse Subs franchisee. “We’re thrilled to celebrate with a fantastic afternoon, including a free Hook & Ladder sub for the first 200 guests, a Calgary Flames ticket giveaway, and a grant ceremony for our local fire station. Supporting this community and the first responders who keep it safe is what this brand has always been about.” The opening supports Firehouse Subs broader growth strategy across Canada, underpinned by operational efficiency, innovative restaurant design and comprehensive franchisee support. “We’re so proud to open our 200th restaurant in Canada,” said Mike Hancock, President of Firehouse Subs. “Nobody makes a hot sub better than we do, and we love bringing our sandwiches to new communities. The part that matters most to me is what this growth does for our Public Safety Foundation. Across Canada, our restaurants and guests have helped fund more than $6.3 million in lifesaving equipment for first responders. To celebrate our 200th opening, we’re donating $54,389 to the local Redwood Meadows Fire Station, which suffered a devastating station fire at the end of 2025. The funds will help replace hydrant related equipment lost in the blaze. Every new restaurant means we can do even more for the people who keep our communities safe.” That support reflects the Firehouse Subs brand’s longstanding commitment to first responders, a mission that extends across North America. To date, the Firehouse Subs Public Safety Foundation has awarded more than $115 million in lifesaving equipment and resources. Ruby Slipper is leaning into the unexpected this fall with a playful mix of flavors. The menu pairs creamy peanut butter with smoky bacon, brings Crescent City heat to a smashburger with Patton’s hot sausage, and gives classic beignets a fall twist with candied apples. A pair of burgers raise the creative bar by taking a familiar favorite in two very different directions. The Yo Mama’s Peanut Butter Bacon Burger ($15) is exactly what it sounds like: a double smashed beef patty topped with creamy peanut butter, Applewood-smoked bacon and American cheese on a brioche bun. For a distinctly New Orleans vibe, the Patton’s Hot Sausage Smashburger ($15) pairs a smashed beef patty with a Patton’s hot sausage patty, pepper jack, Creole mustard aioli, lettuce, tomato and pickled red onions. The Patty Melt ($15) keeps things classic with a double smashed beef patty, American and pepper jack cheeses, caramelized onions and remoulade before getting griddled on sourdough, while the Kale Chicken Caesar ($18) brings together chopped kale, grilled chicken, parmesan, breadcrumbs, lemon and Caesar dressing. On the sweeter side, Ruby Slipper is giving its beignets an early-fall makeover with Candied Apple Beignets ($7.25), served with candied apple compote, vanilla mascarpone and apple cider caramel. The drink menu shakes things up, too. The Apple Cider Mule ($10.50) combines vodka, apple compote, apple cider, ginger beer and lime, while the Whipped Strawberry Mimosa ($11.50) layers strawberry purée, lemon, coconut, sparkling wine and cold foam. Also returning is the Bubbles & Berries ($20), Ruby Slipper’s sparkling bottle service, served with pomegranate watermelon, orange and blueberry lavender juices, blueberry compote and fresh strawberries. “We got a little playful in the kitchen recently, challenging each other to give our guests some delicious combinations they might not expect from us,” said Chef Marla Chua, culinary director for Ruby Slipper. “The savory dishes give the menu more of a lunch feel, while the fall offerings gave us a chance to experiment with some of the flavors we love most about the change of seasons.” The early fall menu will be available at participating Ruby Slipper locations from Sept. 2 through Sept. 29, while supplies last. Across a 50+ location system, however, even the strongest intuition benefits from a clearer view of what is happening across the business. Data provides that context. AI can help interpret it. The opportunity is not to replace experienced operators with algorithms. It is to augment their judgment by helping them recognize important signals earlier, understand what may be driving them, and focus attention where action is most likely to improve the outcome. Tuning Operations to Demand Restaurant demand changes constantly by location, channel, daypart, promotion, weather, and local market conditions. The challenge is translating those signals into practical decisions across labor, production, inventory, and the guest experience. POS transaction data shows what guests are ordering, where demand is occurring, and which channels are driving volume. When combined with labor, inventory, loyalty, financial, and external market data, those signals provide a stronger basis for adjusting operations. A regional leader may identify that a promotion is increasing traffic but slowing kitchen throughput. An operations team may see digital demand growing faster than front-counter demand in a particular market. A concept leader may find that certain menu items perform differently by customer segment or daypart. Cloud-based data warehouse and analytics solutions, which consolidate multiple sources of data, can help bring this information together. Embedded AI can further reduce the analytical burden by surfacing meaningful exceptions rather than requiring operators to search through reports. Empowering Your Team The systems employees use every day affect productivity, training, retention, and guest experience. During a rush, every unnecessary step, confusing screen, or unclear prompt creates friction. The best employee experiences are simple, intuitive, and designed around the task at hand. They present relevant information at the right moment, use consistent interaction patterns, and reduce the training required to complete routine work. Good design also makes complex systems feel simpler. Instead of showing every available option, the experience should prioritize the most relevant actions and reveal additional detail only when needed. This becomes increasingly important as AI enters operational workflows. AI should not appear as another disconnected tool. It should fit naturally into the experience, provide useful context, and help employees complete their work. Used effectively, technology reduces cognitive and administrative effort so employees can spend more time serving guests and supporting their teams. Cost Management When margins tighten, the key questions are where, why, and what action should be taken. Consolidated purchasing and inventory data can reveal fragmented spending, pricing variances, unusual usage, recurring waste, and potential stockouts. The strategic benefit is managing by exception rather than asking operations teams to inspect every item and location manually. Menu engineering should also consider more than popularity. Strong decisions connect sales velocity and contribution margin with food cost, labor requirements, ingredient availability, preparation complexity, and guest behavior. Menu affinity data can show which items appeal to specific customer segments or lookalike groups, helping operators create menus and offers that improve both margin and visit frequency. Third-party market data can add context by showing whether underperformance reflects an execution issue or a broader shift in demand. Labor decisions benefit from timely information as well. Oakwell, which calls itself a “social day spa,” combines the private spa suite experience with a craft beer-and-wine taproom. On a rainy day in Zakopane, Poland, Jessica and Damien Zouaoui went looking for something to do indoors. The newly married New Yorkers were in the middle of an indefinite around-the-world trip after quitting their corporate jobs. They were looking for a business idea—something in hospitality, something scalable, and ideally something Americans had not seen a hundred times before. A beer spa popped up on TripAdvisor. Thirty minutes later, they were soaking in a tub infused with hops and barley, with a keg of Polish beer nearby. That moment became the starting point for Oakwell Beer Spa, the Denver-based hospitality concept that combines private spa suites with a craft beer-and-wine taproom. It is, at first glance, a pairing built to make people raise an eyebrow. Beer and wellness do not exactly live next door to each other in the American imagination. But Oakwell is not trying to turn a spa visit into a bar crawl. It is built around a different idea: Beer can be part of an experience without being the entire point of it. That distinction is becoming more important as restaurants, bars, breweries, and other hospitality businesses look for ways to give consumers a reason to leave the house, and a reason to stay awhile once they arrive. “We both quit our corporate jobs at the same time,” Jessica says. “We sold everything we owned in New York. We packed two backpacks and we headed off on an indefinite round-the-world trip. And the plan was that we weren’t going to come home until we found the perfect business idea.” Damien had worked in sales and marketing within hospitality and travel, while Jessica’s background was in HR and operations. They knew they wanted to build something together, but not another restaurant or coffee shop. Franchising was part of the plan from the beginning. “We never wanted to be a mom-and-pop business owner,” Jessica says. “We were looking for something that was scalable, but also something that we could be passionate about and really excited about.” Their trip through 25 countries became an informal research expedition. After Poland, they began paying closer attention to spa culture elsewhere: onsens in Japan, jjimjilbangs in South Korea, and wine spas in France and Spain. What stood out was not simply the novelty of bathing with beer ingredients. It was the social nature of the experience. In many places, spas were communal, multigenerational, and accessible—not the solitary, expensive, female-skewing luxury service Americans often picture. “Spas are not just for the wealthy,” Jessica says. “Wellness is something that you do as a social experience.” The couple landed in Denver in January 2019 with their backpacks and a business plan. It took more than two years to find space, secure financing, and build the first Oakwell location. The founders did much of the early construction themselves, relying on Home Depot materials and a lean budget. They opened in February 2021, in the middle of a still-unsettled pandemic landscape. “Very quickly, when we launched, we were fully booked seven days a week from 8 a.m. to 11 p.m.,” Damien says. “People were really intrigued about the experience.” Today, Oakwell has two Denver-area locations, including a newer Highlands Ranch store designed as a more polished prototype for franchisees. As it pursues operators in markets including Kansas City, the company is looking to replicate the playbook it has refined at its corporate locations: high-touch hospitality, a distinctive beverage program, and a spa experience built for groups rather than solo indulgence. articles.title: Lola Beans Signs Deal to Grow Into Delaware in Family Affair
articles.titleKo: Lola Beans Signs Deal to Grow Into Delaware in Family Affair
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . It also marks a new chapter for two brothers who have watched each other build careers, families and now, businesses. For Lola Beans founder Donny Bradley, the latest franchise deal is a little more personal than most. The growing drive-thru beverage brand has signed a six-unit franchise agreement to expand into Delaware with Donny’s brother, Jay Bradley, and his wife, Beth. The deal brings Lola Beans back to a place that already means something to the Bradley family. Donny and Jay grew up in Dover, Delaware, while their father was stationed at Dover Air Force Base, and Jay has continued to call Delaware home. Beth was born and raised in Delaware. Eight years ago, Jay & Beth moved 5 miles north, right over the line from the Delaware border to Southern Chester County, PA. Being a stone’s throw away from the DE/PA, we will always call Delaware home. It also marks a new chapter for two brothers who have watched each other build careers, families and now, businesses. Both found careers in the medical industry, with Donny previously working in medical device sales and Jay currently serving as a National Trainer for a spine biologics company. For Jay, bringing Lola Beans to Delaware is an opportunity to build something meaningful alongside his wife in a community they already know and love. Together, they plan to grow the concept throughout the state, bringing the same sense of connection, energy and community they have watched Donny and Missy build in Tennessee. “I’ve had a front-row seat to Lola Beans from the beginning, and I’ve watched Donny and Missy build something that is genuinely different,” said Jay Bradley. “It’s fun, it’s positive and it’s centered around making people’s day better. My wife and I are excited to bring that same energy to Delaware and build something our family can be proud of here.” “Watching Donny & Missy’s journey in Lola Beans inspired us….we have always wished we lived closer to them, so starting this new chapter gives us a little bit of our Chattanooga Family right here in Delaware/Pennsylvania.” “There’s something really special about your own family believing in what you’ve built enough to want to become part of it,” said Donny Bradley, co-founder of Lola Beans. “Jay has seen Lola Beans from the very beginning. He knows the hard work and everything that has gone into building it. For him and his family to say, ‘We want to bring this to Delaware,’ means a lot to Missy and me.” Donny’s career in medical device sales ultimately played an unexpected role in the Lola Beans story. In 2014, his work took him, Missy and their family to Soldotna, Alaska, where they became regulars at the area’s small drive-thru coffee huts. What stuck with them was the genuine connection and the way a quick interaction could turn around someone’s day. That experience eventually became the inspiration for Lola Beans. Donny and Missy opened the first Lola Beans in Chattanooga in 2020, followed by a second company-owned location in Cleveland, Tennessee. Today, they continue to invest in the concept themselves, with additional corporate growth planned in Tennessee alongside the brand’s franchise expansion. The Delaware agreement marks the latest step in that growth, bringing Lola Beans back to where the Bradley brothers’ story began while carrying the brand’s focus on good energy, genuine connection and community into a new state. articles.title: The Real Lesson in McDonald’s 515-Page Loyalty File
articles.titleKo: The Real Lesson in McDonald’s 515-Page Loyalty File
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . What unsettled the reporter wasn’t that McDonald’s had his data. It was seeing the backend terms laid bare. Last month, WIRED published an article from a reporter who requested his own McDonald’s loyalty data and was shocked when he got back 515 pages: every Monopoly prize he’d ever won, a predicted 2.16 visits over the next six weeks, an average order of $13.49, and a churn score of zero. He asked McDonald’s to delete his file and stopped eating there just to see if he could prove the algorithm wrong. The internet had a field day with just how much McDonald’s knew about the reporter. But if you run a restaurant with a loyalty program, chances are you are sitting on some version of this same data. The real question isn’t whether you have it. It’s whether you’re using it to make a guest feel actually known or just tracked. Guest data is a trade, not a form of surveillance Think of loyalty as a transaction, and data is the currency the guest spends. It’s the only currency a brand wants more than money, because it’s what makes better business decisions possible. That’s not a controversial take, even among the WIRED article’s readers. For example, several commenters shrugged at the McDonald’s report: tracking and forecasting purchases is a legitimate business case, and companies have been profiling regulars since the department store credit card. (One reader turned the question back on the outlet, asking whether WIRED could say what it stores on its own subscribers.) The reporter’s 515-page file is really a receipt for years of purchases. In exchange for reporting what he ate and when, he got perks and points that added up (and let’s not forget those Monopoly prizes). Both sides paid. Both sides collected. What unsettled the reporter wasn’t that McDonald’s had his data. It was seeing the backend terms laid bare, things like “attrition likelihood” and “RFM-derived top product.” Strip away the jargon, and 515 pages of transaction history built up over several years is a fairly ordinary amount of data. It’s what any brand needs to market effectively, forecast demand, and stay competitive in today’s environment. Creating personalized loyalty I worked in restaurants for 15 years before building software, and I lived the analog version of loyalty rewards. We’d walk regulars to their usual booths and have their favorite drinks waiting for them before they asked. In return, these guests gave us their feedback and their business. They didn’t feel watched. They felt known. Recreating that kind of personalized experience at scale used to require an entire team of analysts that only the biggest chains could afford. Most restaurant brands, even successful multi-unit ones, never had the resources to know a single guest that well, let alone act on it. Because of technology, that’s no longer true. A modern guest engagement platform builds one profile per guest across every ordering channel, then segments guests automatically by how recently, how often, and how much they’ve ordered. That segmentation is what turns “hasn’t ordered in 60 days” into an automatic win-back offer, or “always orders the same wrap” into a birthday reward that isn’t generic. Operators don’t need McDonald’s scale to do this anymore. They just need the right digital platform. A known guest who has offered their data should get something a stranger to the brand cannot buy: Order preferences that carry across channels, so they never have to re-enter them A pickup order that’s labeled with their name, thanking them for being a loyal guest First access to a limited item before it hits the full menu A comped item that shows up the day after a bad visit, unprompted, because the brand noticed Every one of these requires knowing the guest. Every one is worth more to that guest than another 15 percent off, and most cost the brand less to deliver than a blanket dis

SupplyCaddy has received growth investment from CEAS Investments, which is a partner in the business. Established in 2020, SupplyCaddy supplies customised packaging and supply chain services to restaurant groups. It currently works with more than 70 brands, among them sweetgreen, Dave’s Hot Chicken, Huey Magoo’s and Burger King, covering over 6,500 sites in North America and nine overseas markets. The business collaborates with foodservice distribution groups such as Sysco, US Foods, Gordon Food Service, Performance Food Group, Imperial Dade and McLane. SupplyCaddy CEO and co-founder Zachary Stein said: “For six years, Bradley and I have been building a company that puts relationships ahead of transactions and long-term partnerships ahead of short-term wins. “We did not set out to create another packaging company. We wanted to be the kind of partner restaurant brands deserve: one that understands their business, anticipates challenges and cares about their success as deeply as they do. This investment gives us additional resources to continue building that company at a much larger scale.” SupplyCaddy said it continues to operate under its founders, with Stein and co-founder Bradley Saveth retaining oversight of commercial ties and remaining directly engaged with each restaurant brand on its client list. The new funding aims to support a wider manufacturing footprint in domestic and overseas markets. It will also help ramp up work on packaging innovation, engineering and sustainable materials, and further investment in technology, logistics and supply chain systems. The company added that the capital is also to be used for inventory planning, customer support, hiring in sourcing, operations and product development, and expansion into additional international markets. With the additional funding, the company intends to support restaurant brands in developing more resilient supply chains, expediting product development, and managing increasingly complex packaging programmes. CEAS Investments chief investment officer Mike Wohl said: “When we first invested in SupplyCaddy, we saw a talented management team with a clear vision for addressing a significant and evolving need within the restaurant industry. “Bradley, Zachary and the entire SupplyCaddy team have continued to distinguish themselves through disciplined execution, deep customer relationships and an uncommon level of founder involvement. They have built more than a packaging company. They have created a scalable global platform capable of becoming one of the restaurant industry’s most trusted packaging and supply chain partners.” The post SupplyCaddy Receives Growth Infusion from Partner CEAS Investments appeared first on QSR Magazine .

Grimaldi’s Pizzeria, the award-winning Brooklyn-style pizzeria known for its coal-fired, brick-oven pizza, today announced the sale of its Bell Tower Fort Myers location to UNIV Hospitality of Fort Myers, LLC, led by principals Gary Patel and Anil Harkhani. In connection with the acquisition, UNIV Hospitality has entered into a franchise development agreement with Grimaldi’s to open five additional restaurants across Sarasota, Lee and Collier counties, expanding the brand’s presence throughout Southwest Florida. The agreement marks Grimaldi’s continued franchise growth and expands the brand’s presence in Florida, bringing its signature pizzas, calzones and other fan favorites to additional markets across the state. Southwest Florida is the third domestic franchise territory for Grimaldi’s, joining Alabama and Iowa, as Grimaldi’s continues expansion across the United States, as well as internationally. “We’re excited to welcome Gary, Anil and the UNIV Hospitality team to the Grimaldi’s franchise family,” said Michael A. Flaum, COO of Grimaldi’s Pizzeria. “Their experience and commitment to hospitality make them a strong partner as we continue to grow the Grimaldi’s brand.” “With the acquisition of Grimaldi’s Bell Tower restaurant and plans to expand across Southwest Florida, we look forward to building on the restaurant’s success and bringing Grimaldi’s to even more communities throughout the region,” said Anil Harkhani, UNIV Hospitality. “We plan to bring the same family-friendly, casual yet upscale atmosphere and award-winning pizzas to communities across southwest Florida.” Grimaldi’s is known for its coal-fired, brick-oven pizza and calzones, made with a secret recipe dough, sliced fresh mozzarella cheese and techniques dating back to more than 100 years in Brooklyn. Guests can also enjoy salads, starters and desserts, including Grimaldi’s famous house-made New York Style Cheesecake. The Bell Tower restaurant is located in Fort Myers, Florida, and will continue to operate under the Grimaldi’s Pizzeria brand as part of the UNIV Hospitality portfolio. Award-winning hospitality group Noble 33 announces Mr. Noble, an American brasserie concept built around upscale comfort food set to debut in Chicago’s River North neighborhood in early 2027. Located at 500 N. Clark St., the two-level restaurant will feature a lively restaurant upstairs and a subterranean speakeasy below, creating two distinct experiences under one roof. Mr. Noble is the second Chicago concept announced by Noble 33, following plans for a new Mexican-inspired concept slated for Fulton Market. Together, the two projects mark Noble 33’s entry into Chicago across two of the city’s most dynamic neighborhoods, each with its own distinct culinary point of view. “This is one of the most serious food cities in the country, and that’s exactly why we didn’t want to bring in something we’d already built somewhere else and just put a River North address on it,” said Noble 33 Co-Founder Tosh Berman. “Mr. Noble is a brand-new concept for Noble 33, and we’re excited for it to become Chicago’s own.” Mr. Noble will introduce a new category to Noble 33’s growing global portfolio, marking the hospitality group’s first concept centered around upscale American comfort food. The new brand joins Noble 33’s acclaimed collection, from Los Angeles to London, including Mēdüzā Mediterrania, Sparrow Italia, Toca Madera, Casa Madera and 1587 Prime. Upstairs at Mr. Noble, familiar dishes get steakhouse-level sourcing and technique, served with the ease of a neighborhood tavern. Downstairs, the mood shifts entirely as a dim, sultry speakeasy with live vocals gives guests a reason to make an entire evening out of their visit. The address itself has a storied place in River North’s dining history. Most recently, the space was home to Jaleo by chef José Andrés, which opened in 2021 and closed in January 2025, along with its basement speakeasy, Pigtail. Before that, the address was home to Michelin-starred restaurant Naha. “The moment we walked the space, we saw the potential,” said Noble 33 Co-Founder and CEO Mikey Tanha. “The building has character, history, and a two-level layout that let us build the framework for something we think River North is going to gather at for years to come.” The property is part of Friedman Properties’ longstanding River North portfolio. The family-run developer has played an integral role in the evolution of the neighborhood for more than five decades. “We’re excited to welcome Noble 33’s Mr. Noble to River North, further demonstrating the neighborhood’s staying power as Chicago’s most diverse and vibrant dining destination,” said Albert Friedman, chairman and CEO of Friedman Properties. “The addition of this national hospitality group complements the area’s established mix of dining, hospitality, office, residential and entertainment offerings and reflects its continued ability to attract new energy and investment.” For more information, visit noble33.com or follow @noble.33 on Instagram. articles.title: The Flying Biscuit Café Inks Franchise Deal in McDonough, Georgia

articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . The Flying Biscuit Café has signed a franchise agreement with franchisee Keisha Carter to bring the Atlanta-born all-day breakfast and brunch brand to McDonough, Ga., and the surrounding Henry County market. The site and opening date will be announced separately. Henry County is one of the fastest-growing counties in Georgia. Its population rose from 203,922 residents in 2010 to 240,712 in the 2020 census, and the U.S. Census Bureau estimated it at 264,922 in 2025. McDonough, the county seat and its largest city, sits along Interstate 75 about 30 miles southeast of downtown Atlanta. Carter, who lives in the market, said growth there has outpaced the area’s sit-down breakfast and brunch options — the gap that drew her to it. Carter brings nearly 10 years of experience in sales, business development, operations, client relations and team leadership, including roles at several Fortune 500 companies before moving into entrepreneurship. She holds an MBA in finance management and is a Six Sigma Black Belt, and currently leads a metro Atlanta real estate group where she oversees business operations, marketing, sales strategy, team development and client experience. She and her family have been Flying Biscuit regulars for years, and often talked about the south metro needing a location closer to home. Carter will partner with Eric Gladmon, who will serve as the venture’s main operating partner. Gladmon owns and operates an Atlanta salon that has been in business for more than 30 years, and brings that ownership and operations experience to the group. “Flying Biscuit has been an Atlanta staple and a longtime favorite for us as Georgia natives with deep roots in the area, so choosing a brand we already knew and loved felt natural,” said Keisha Carter, franchisee of the McDonough Flying Biscuit Café. “What makes this journey especially meaningful is that we get to do it as a family. After losing my mom in 2022, there’s something incredibly special about building this next chapter alongside my husband and my cousin, who shared such a close relationship with her. We’re excited to welcome the McDonough community into what we hope will feel like an extension of our own family.” The agreement covers one café, in McDonough. Carter has said she hopes to develop additional Flying Biscuit cafés in Georgia communities over time. She has also identified catering as a focus, pointing to Henry County’s school system, Piedmont Henry Hospital, local colleges, corporate offices, distribution centers and community organizations as potential customers. “Atlanta is where this brand started, and we’re still filling in pieces of the metro — Henry County is one of them,” said Andrew Scherzer, partner and director of franchise development for Flying Biscuit Franchising. “Keisha spent years wishing there were a Flying Biscuit closer to home, and now she’s the one bringing it. Operators who come to us as guests first tend to get the details right.” The McDonough café will serve The Flying Biscuit Café’s full breakfast and lunch menu, including its biscuits, shrimp and grits, omelets, vegan scrambles, burgers and wraps, along with full-service catering. The location, opening date and hiring details will be announced separately. More information about the brand is at flyingbiscuit.com. Prospective operators can find available markets, ownership requirements and how to start a conversation with the development team at flyingbiscuitfranchising.com. articles.title: The Case for Real Food: Why We Need the Salad More Than Ever
articles.titleKo: The Case for Real Food: Why We Need the Salad More Than Ever
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Real food doesn't need to reinvent itself to stay relevant. In recent weeks, the headlines have been heavy. Concerns regarding food safety have understandably caused many of us to pause, look at our plates and ask questions about where our food comes from and how it’s handled. These questions as not just necessary, but vital. When the world feels uncertain, I find myself returning to the basics. The most important decision any of us makes each day isn’t about our schedule or our to-do list — it’s the choice of how we fuel our bodies. Why Salads Still Matter We live in an era of ultra-processed convenience. While these options are fast, they often lack the foundational nutrients our bodies require to thrive. Consider that many grab-and-go meals are engineered for shelf life and speed, not for what they deliver nutritionally – a trade off most of us make without even realizing it. A well-constructed salad is the antithesis of this since it’s a powerhouse of nutrient density, delivering an unparalleled concentration of health-promoting compounds in every bite: Essential Micronutrients: Leafy greens and colorful vegetables carry vitamins A, C, and K, along with iron, folate, and potassium. These are the basics our immune systems and hearts actually depend on, and they’re the same nutrients most commonly missing from a fast-food value meal or a vending machine lunch. High-Impact Fiber : Fiber is the one nutrient most people underrate. It keeps digestion steady, blood sugar level, and it’s the reason a good salad keeps you full for hours instead of one. Most adults fall short of recommended daily fiber intake, and a single well-built salad can close a meaningful part of that gap in one sitting. Powerful Antioxidants: Antioxidants like lutein and beta-carotene fight the inflammation that builds up over time and support our eyes, our brains, our long-term health. These compounds don’t just protect against disease down the road, they are linked to sharper focus and steadier energy right now, which matters as much at 2 p.m. at your desk as it does decades from now. Bioavailability : Pair your greens with healthy fats like olive oil, avocado, or nuts, and you absorb more of those nutrients. It’s not just a salad at that point — it’s a system working the way it’s supposed to. That’s also why the format matters as much as the ingredients: a salad thrown together without any fat or protein leaves most of its potential on the table, while a thoughtfully composed one turns simple produce into something the body can actually use. Why the Salad is More Relevant Than Ever I still eat a salad most days. This isn’t because I have to, but because it’s one of the few decisions in our days that is entirely in our control. In a season full of headlines none of us can control, this matters more than it used to. This is why, despite the challenges facing our food system, the salad remains the gold standard. It’s a tool for personal control, allowing people to tailor their intake of lean proteins, healthy fats, and complex carbohydrates to meet their own goals — without ever sacrificing well-being for the sake of speed. Rebuilding Trust Through Transparency The recent wave of food safety headlines has shaken consumer confidence and some of that skepticism has been fair. Too often, “fresh” has been used as a marketing label instead of an operational standard. Rebuilding trust starts with transparency: knowing exactly where produce comes from, how it’s handled from farm to store and how many hands it passes through before it reaches a guest’s bowl. For us, this means shorter, more accountable supply chains; consistent, verifiable food-safety protocols across every location and a willingness to talk openly with guests about sourcing and handling, rather than treating it like a trade secret. In this environment, silence reads as evasion.

Fractured Prune Doughnuts has spent 50 years building its name around a simple promise. The doughnuts don’t hit the fryer until the customer walks through the door. Now CEO Danny Windon wants to see how far that formula can travel. The made-to-order doughnut concept is preparing for a new round of franchise expansion after completing a new franchise disclosure document in March. Fractured Prune currently has 15 restaurants, including five owned by Windon, and began marketing franchise opportunities around Memorial Day. The stores are based in Maryland, New Jersey, and Delaware. The early response has given Windon plenty to sort through. Fractured Prune has received more than 100 inquiries since launching its franchise push, which Windon has narrowed to roughly 45 serious prospects. He isn’t chasing a specific unit target. “I’m not looking for dots on a map or an arbitrary number as my goal,” he says. “I want to find the right people and the right fit that have the same drive as I do and passion for the product because those are the people—just like the good bartenders that can pack a bar—those are the people that are going to bring people in.” That outlook comes from Windon’s own path through the system. His first career was as an elementary school teacher before he moved into residential real estate and later commercial real estate. In 2007, with the real estate market starting to deteriorate, Windon visited an existing Fractured Prune with a friend. He liked the doughnut. Then the franchisee asked whether Windon and his friend wanted to buy the store. They did. What began as a side venture grew into eight Fractured Prune locations within five years. Windon spent the ensuing years running the restaurants himself, moving from store to store and learning the operational model firsthand. “I ran every single store every day. I was in and out of the stores completely hands on. I didn’t have managers and things like that. I was just popping in and out the entire time,” Windon says. His relationship with the brand changed again at the end of 2019, when he acquired the entire franchise system. Two months later, COVID disrupted the restaurant industry and delayed his plans for the concept. Windon spent the following years working on the business before putting the pieces in place for a renewed franchise push in 2025. He began assembling the new FDD last fall and completed it in March. His experience as a franchisee has influenced how he wants the franchisor-franchisee relationship to function. Windon sees operators as a source of ideas because they interact with guests every day and hear firsthand what customers want. “Your franchisees, they’re basically your ground troops. So they’re hearing everything. They’re hearing what people are asking for. It’s super important to give them a voice be able to say, ‘Hey, people are asking about this. Can we try it and give it a shot?’” Windon says. That feedback can lead to menu additions, but Windon has two pieces of the Fractured Prune model he considers non-negotiable: hot, made-to-order doughnuts and the guest experience surrounding them. The concept’s customization model gives customers a choice between roughly 22 established combinations or building their own creation. Guests select from at least 19 glazes and 22 toppings and candies, with seasonal choices added throughout the year. Customers can add as many toppings as they want for the same price. Fractured Prune doesn’t begin cooking the doughnut until an order is placed. That distinction has survived as competitors and other customizable doughnut concepts have emerged. Pancheros Mexican Grill, the Iowa-born, fresh-Mex concept known for its fresh-pressed tortillas and delicious queso, will continue planting its Iowa roots with a new location coming to Waukee next week. Opening on Tuesday, September 8, the new Waukee restaurant marks the third restaurant for longtime Pancheros franchisees, Shelly and Tyson Robinson. After assuming ownership of the West Des Moines and Johnston locations from Shelly’s father nearly a decade ago, the Robinsons will now expand their footprint with a new location, with their existing locations both recently celebrating 20+ years in business. Their continued partnership demonstrates the local family’s investment in the brand, as well as the growing demand for more Pancheros locations in Iowa after more than 34 years of serving guests and building fandom throughout the state. “As an Iowa native that grew up with Pancheros, having the opportunity to grow this brand within the local community is incredibly fulfilling,” said Shelly Robinson, franchisee of the new Waukee restaurant and the Johnston and West Des Moines locations. “We’re proud to keep growing with a brand so many love and to continue investing in Waukee and the greater Des Moines community that we’re so proud to call home.” Since joining the Pancheros franchise system more than two decades ago, Shelly and her family have built a strong presence in the communities they serve. The Robinsons have made local involvement a consistent part of their business, including supporting youth sports programs throughout the region by providing meals for local teams and hosting Queso for a Cause events to raise funds for local causes. In addition to the new Waukee location, the Robinsons recently celebrated 21 years of serving guests at the West Des Moines location and 20 years at the Johnston location. The Johnston restaurant will also soon undergo a full remodel, including refreshed flooring and interior finishes, as well as the addition of a second make line designed to streamline digital orders. The Waukee Pancheros will be located at 2980 Grand Prairie Pkwy #100 Waukee, IA 50263 and will be open from 10:30 a.m. – 10 p.m. daily. This location will feature approximately 2,600 square feet of kitchen and dining space, offering Pancheros’ signature burritos made with fresh-pressed tortillas, marinated and grilled proteins and house-made salsas, all mixed together evenly using Bob the Tool—a proprietary spatula created by the brand—to ensure every bite is the perfect bite.. The restaurant will also include a mobile pick-up/drive-thru window, designated parking for digital orders, and a second make-line. Following the September 8 opening, the new Waukee location will offer $1 burritos for loyalty members from September 15-19. Locals can secure their $1 burrito by downloading the Pancheros app, selecting “MORE,” then “COUPON” and entering code “KEETOWN1” where prompted. 1,000 codes will be available in total. Extras are still extra. The new Waukee location will also participate in Pancheros’ September Queso Challenge, allowing loyalty members to earn half off an entrée after ordering queso four times during the month. The location will also honor Pancheros’ National Queso Day offer on September 20, when loyalty members can receive free queso on their entrée. Vandelay Companies continues its growth across Texas and beyond with the opening of its Hudson House Southlake location, bringing the group’s East Coast–inspired neighborhood restaurant to Southlake on Monday, September 14. Located at 1131 E. Southlake Blvd., the new approximately 5,000-square-foot restaurant represents another step in the continued expansion of one of Vandelay Companies’ most established concepts. Since opening the original Hudson House in Highland Park, the brand has grown from a Dallas neighborhood restaurant into a defining concept within the Vandelay portfolio, earning a loyal following for lunch, brunch, dinner and its celebrated happy hour. The brand’s continued growth reflects Vandelay Companies’ broader approach to expansion: identifying strong neighborhoods and markets, investing in each restaurant for the long term and building concepts designed to become lasting parts of the communities they serve. “Hudson House has exploded because we have remained disciplined about where and how we expand it,” said Hunter Pond, Founder & Chairman of Vandelay Companies. “Southlake has the combination of energy, growth and appreciation for hospitality that we look for when entering a new neighborhood. Our goal is never simply to add another location. We want every Hudson House to feel rooted in its community from the moment it opens and to become the kind of restaurant guests return to week after week.” Known for its polished interpretation of a classic East Coast neighborhood restaurant, Hudson House combines a seafood-driven menu, expansive raw bar, sushi, signature cocktails and timeless American favorites within a warm, energetic setting. Among the restaurant’s best-known dishes are Hudson’s Avocado Dip, made with whipped avocado, green onion, herbs and ranch chips; The Cheeseburger, featuring thin patties, American cheese, pickles and Hudson’s signature house sauce; Chicken Parm, served with creamy tomato pasta and Reggiano; and the Hudson Salad, made with popcorn chicken, avocado, cherry tomato, bacon, sharp cheddar and green goddess dressing. Hudson House’s seafood program remains central to the experience, with East Coast oysters flown in daily, a dedicated raw bar and a sushi menu that includes the Sunset Roll, with spicy tuna, cucumber and avocado topped with salmon, lemon and ginger vinaigrette; the riceless Signature Roll, featuring salmon, tuna, crab, avocado, tempura flake and spicy ponzu; the Pressed Ahi Tuna Roll, with tuna sashimi, spicy tuna, avocado, spicy mayo, eel sauce and truffle oil; and Spicy Tuna Crispy Rice with chili mayo and eel sauce. The beverage program is equally defining, led by Hudson House’s signature “World’s Coldest Martini,” featuring Grey Goose vodka served on tap and chilled to a crisp 10 degrees for an exceptionally cold, smooth pour. Martini selections include The Classic, Bleu & Gold, made with vodka, olive juice, bleu cheese salt and housemade bleu cheese olives; The Lemon Drop, finished with limoncello foam; and The Espresso, made with vodka, espresso, Kahlúa and Baileys. Additional cocktail favorites include the Frozen Bellini, Strawberry Spritz, Spicy Mexican and a classic Manhattan. The Southlake restaurant will bring Hudson House’s signature design language to a larger neighborhood setting, featuring warm leather booths, a large wraparound bar, a spacious sit-down raw bar and an outdoor patio. The space is designed to balance the familiarity of a traditional New England dining institution with the polished, energetic atmosphere that has become synonymous with the Hudson House brand. Guests can enjoy: Smoked Salmon Benny: Olive-oil-brushed focaccia layered with herbed cream cheese, smoked salmon and poached cage-free eggs, finished with cream cheese hollandaise, pickled red onions and lemon olive gremolata. Smothered Breakfast Burrito: Cage-free scrambled eggs, hash browns, black beans, sautéed onions and poblanos wrapped in a flour tortilla and smothered in red and green chile with lime crema. Breakfast Tacos: Three corn tortillas filled with cage-free scrambled eggs, melted cheeses and sautéed onions and poblanos, finished with lime crema and served with hash browns, fire-roasted pico and jalapeño avocado salsa. articles.titleKo: Sweetgreen Brings Back Fall Harvest Menu

To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . sweetgreen has announced the nationwide return of its Fall Harvest menu, the brand’s largest limited-time menu, featuring the fan-favorite Autumn Harvest Bowl alongside two new seasonal offerings: the Maple Glazed Salmon plate and Roasted Bacon Brussels side. The launch is supported by “Fall’s Best Dressed,” a new campaign that spotlights sweetgreen’s beloved maple-glazed brussels sprouts as the season’s most craveable side. To celebrate the return, sweetgreen is giving its maple-glazed brussels sprouts the full fashion treatment. “Fall’s Best Dressed,” a new campaign starring actors Jack Falahee and Maia Reficco, draws inspiration from fashion editorials and annual best-dressed lists to put the unlikely fall style icon in the spotlight. Styled by Ryan Young, the campaign will run nationwide across select paid, social and out-of-home channels. “Every fall has an ‘it’ item. Ours happens to be brussels sprouts,” said Zipporah Allen, Chief Commercial Officer at sweetgreen. “Only sweetgreen can take something like a brussels sprout and turn it into an object of desire by dressing them with our crave-worthy maple glaze. Jack and Maia brought exactly the right mix of style and playfulness to co-star alongside a seasonal favorite in a completely new way.” “Brussels sprouts are genuinely my favorite vegetable, so I didn’t need much convincing,” said Falahee. “Giving them a best-dressed campaign felt appropriately over the top. They’re crispy, maple-glazed and, frankly, ready for their close-up.” “Fashion is one of the ways I play with character and mood; whether that’s through acting, music, or theatre, so I loved bringing that same energy somewhere completely unexpected,” said Reficco. “After learning how important brussel sprouts were to sweetgreen and what their creative vision was to highlight them, I was instantly on board.” Fall Harvest has become a defining part of the season at sweetgreen. It is the highest-volume limited-time offering in company history, with more than 1.4 million Autumn Harvest Bowls sold across its 2024 and 2025 seasons. The 2026 Fall Harvest menu includes: Autumn Harvest Bowl – A sweet-and-savory seasonal side featuring maple-glazed Brussels sprouts, crumbled bacon and charred jalapeño ranch. Also available without bacon. Maple Glazed Salmon – A new seasonal plate featuring antibiotic-free miso-glazed salmon, maple-glazed brussels, warm roasted sweet potatoes, napa cabbage slaw, white rice and garlic aioli. Roasted Bacon Brussels – A new seasonal side pairing maple-glazed brussels sprouts with crumbled bacon and charred jalapeño ranch. Also available without bacon. The return of sweetgreen’s maple-glazed brussels began long before they hit the menu. This fall, the brand sourced the seasonal ingredient from Dynasty Farms in California’s Santa Maria and Salinas Valleys and Turek Farms, a fourth-generation family farm in New York’s Finger Lakes. Dynasty’s brussels sprouts come from a single ranch, while Turek Farms carries forward its family legacy with a crop that is 100% hand-picked and force-cooled on-site within 24 to 48 hours of harvest. Together, these hands-on practices reflect the care behind one of sweetgreen’s signature fall ingredients. The Fall Harvest menu is available now at sweetgreen locations nationwide. Guests can order in-store, through the sweetgreen app or online for pickup or delivery. For more information about sweetgreen and its seasonal menu, visit www.swee t green.com and follow @sweetgreen on social media. articles.title: Maybe the Lettuce Isn’t Worth the Crunch
articles.titleKo: Maybe the Lettuce Isn’t Worth the Crunch
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . The 2026 cyclosporiasis outbreak has become the largest recorded in the United States. Two people in Michigan have died, more than 12,000 outbreak-linked cases have been reported in that state alone, and the outbreak has now spread across 15 states. Federal surveillance has lagged some state reporting, but the scale is clear: thousands of confirmed cases, thousands more under investigation, and growing concern among consumers. One major cluster has been traced to shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms operations in central Mexico served at Taco Bell restaurants. Federal officials have linked 1,947 illnesses and at least 98 hospitalizations across nine states to that cluster. The consequences are no longer limited to public-health statistics. U.S. fresh-lettuce unit sales fell 9 percent during one week in July, and Taco Bell foot traffic was down more than 11 percent year over year on August 1 as the outbreak weighed on consumer confidence. For quick-service and fast-casual operators, the immediate issue is food safety. The larger operating question is why lettuce continues to be treated as a cheap, uncomplicated menu staple when its full cost includes refrigeration, spoilage, supply disruption, recall exposure, and brand risk. The restaurant industry has spent the past decade reconsidering nearly everything. Operators have rebuilt ordering systems, redesigned kitchens, introduced new labor models, expanded delivery, created loyalty platforms, adjusted portions, and rewritten menus around shifting costs. Lettuce has remained largely untouched. It is inexpensive, familiar, and expected on burgers, tacos, sandwiches, salads, and bowls. Those qualities have helped it avoid a more complicated question: Is lettuce still worth its full operating cost? Refrigeration Put Lettuce on the American Plate Iceberg lettuce rose alongside the modern American food-distribution system. Its compact, hardy head allowed growers to ship it farther than more delicate greens. California lettuce traveled across the country in ice-packed railcars beginning in the 1920s. The spread of refrigerated transportation, national grocery distribution, and household refrigeration made year-round lettuce increasingly practical. By 1950, iceberg was consumed more than any other vegetable in the United States. The cultivar fit the emerging system well. It was sturdy, standardized, mild, relatively inexpensive, and capable of surviving national transportation. That history explains how lettuce became embedded in American meals. It also illustrates how an operating choice can become a permanent assumption. Once an ingredient becomes broadly available, operators build purchasing contracts, equipment, recipes, portions, and customer expectations around its continued presence. Familiarity gradually begins to resemble necessity. The success of iceberg in the refrigerated supply chains of the twentieth century offers a historical explanation for its popularity. It does not settle whether every twenty-first-century menu still needs to be built around it. “We’ve always done it this way” remains a weak operating principle, even when the original decision made perfect sense. A Recurring Food-Safety Exposure This year’s outbreak is part of a much longer pattern involving leafy greens. A 2024 study published in the Journal of Food Protection estimated that leafy greens account for as much as 9.18% of U.S. foodborne illnesses attributed to identified pathogens. Including illnesses for which no pathogen was identified, the researchers estimated that leafy greens may be associated with approximately 2.3 million illnesses and as much as $5.28 billion in economic costs annually. Chang’s in July 1993 in Scottsdale, Arizona. It’s grown to 20-plus countries and 300 global stores (about 200 in the U.S.) But it had begun to drift through ownership swaps and leadership moves. Mazany was named CEO in November 2025, making him the fourth lead executive in about two years. He succeeded former COO and CFO Brad Hill, who elevated in April and left after a few months. Hill stepped in for ex-Panera Bread chief brand and concept officer Eduardo Luz (today with Pizza Hut). He held the title since October 2023 and followed interim CEO Rohit Manocha, holding a spot vacated when now-Red Lobster CEO Damon Adamolekun departed in early August 2023, ending a tenure dating to 2020. Adamolekun was a partner at private equity firm Paulson & Co., which teamed up with TriArtisan Capital Partners in 2019 to buy P.F. Chang’s for about $700 million. It was previously owned by Centerbridge Partners LP, a group that bought it in 2012 for $1.1 billion. Centerbridge is also the firm that once directed CraftWorks, an entity that ultimately became SPB after Fortress deployed a $93 million credit bid to buy 61 locations and form the group. In plain terms, Mazany saw a brand, he says, in need of believing in itself and what it could be again. “I thought that was a big, big takeaway,” Mazany says. “For me, being a restaurant guy and being a hospitality guy, I felt like I could give this brand a sense of what winning looks like and tap into that pride and heritage of what the brand has always stood for.” Mazany came to the brand with three-plus decades of industry experience. He knew P.F. Chang’s had the roots and equity. There were operators in the field and employees ready to engage. It was more a matter or reenergizing the chain. “And [add] a sense of urgency and purpose,” Mazany says. So, where to begin? P.F. Chang’s average-unit volumes were about $4.2 million as Mazany took over, and the company generated just shy of $1 billion in revenue. For perspective, AUVs were $4.1 million when Centerbridge started exploring a sale those years earlier. Mazany didn’t believe it was a smart approach to examine P.F. Chang’s 200 restaurants and tell everyone what was going wrong. Instead, he outlined what success might look like. “Every guest who comes in is an opportunity to delight and exceed expectations,” he says. “And really good operators always have a principle of the guest experience will never exceed the employee experience. You have to start by building an employee base of people who are committed and who believe in what we do. articles.title: The Evolving Intersection of Delivery Tech, Kitchen Operations, and the Guest Relationship
articles.titleKo: The Evolving Intersection of Delivery Tech, Kitchen Operations, and the Guest Relationship
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . At Mellow Mushroom, an order placed through the brand’s website may still be delivered by a DoorDash Drive courier through a white-label arrangement. More than half a decade after the pandemic fundamentally changed how consumers interact with restaurants, delivery has moved well beyond the “turn it on” phase for full-service operators. The focus now is less on adding a sales channel than on optimizing one that touches the kitchen, labor model, guest relationship, and broader tech stack. “We look at it a little differently nowadays,” says Jason Saposnik, VP of information technology for FSC Franchise Co., the parent company of Beef ‘O’ Brady’s, The Brass Tap, and Newk’s Eatery. “Early on, the focus was more about just growing delivery sales. Now, we’re a lot more focused on whether those sales are profitable, how the restaurants can handle that increased volume, and whether customers are actually getting the same great experience.” The first major improvement in delivery operations was straightforward: getting orders into the restaurant without forcing employees to act as the integration layer. Saposnik recalls an earlier “tablet hell” environment in which teams monitored separate devices for DoorDash, Uber Eats, and other channels, then manually entered orders into the POS. “That created all sorts of issues for missed orders and mistakes and delays,” he says. “Now, everything just flows into the POS and into the kitchen correctly.” That integration is table stakes. But it does not solve underlying capacity questions. Scott Pavlica, VP of finance at Mecha Noodle Bar, says operators need to think beyond delivery as a percentage of sales and focus on the actual volume a restaurant can absorb at its busiest moments. “You have to think about absolutes and how much volume per 15 minutes, per half hour, per hour—whichever metric you have—that you can really handle,” Pavlica says. “You really have to understand what you can actually handle at peak, because that’s where the pressure points start getting applied.” The real test comes when digital demand collides with a packed dining room and the same line, expo station, and staff have to serve both. “When the dining room is full, the guest doesn’t care that we have 20 or 30 or 50 additional orders in that hour coming through the same fixed amount of real estate,” Pavlica says. “At the same time, the digital guest doesn’t care that the dining room is full. They both just want their food.” That is where delivery throttling and kitchen display system prioritization come into play. FSC uses order-volume thresholds to adjust promised delivery times and control when tickets begin appearing in the kitchen. The point is not simply to slow orders down, Saposnik says, but to pace them more accurately around the restaurant’s actual capacity. Those systems still require operational judgment. Managers must account for how the kitchen is performing in real time rather than relying solely on a threshold established in advance. Saposnik sees an opportunity for AI to eventually weigh fulfillment pace, order flow across channels, table turns, and kitchen performance more quickly than a manager can during a rush. But operators are also finding that some of the most consequential delivery improvements have little to do with sophisticated automation. “A lot of the solutions are kind of unsexy,” Pavlica says. “Have you mise en place’d all of your materials to satisfy a to-go order? Just like we want hot plates nearby so we can plate food and get it out, we need our to-go materials to be available in the same manner.” That can mean rethinking storage, giving packaging and labeling supplies a more logical home, or building more space for off-premises production into new units. articles.title: LEON Hires Pret Veteran Julio Santoyo as Managing Director of Restaurants as Part of its Ongoing Commitment to Building “The A-Team”
articles.titleKo: LEON Hires Pret Veteran Julio Santoyo as Managing Director of Restaurants as Part of its Ongoing Commitment to Building “The A-Team”
articles.originalSummary: Julio describes the move as ‘a huge and important opportunity’ LEON founder calls the appointment ‘pivotal’. LEON, the original fast food disrupter, today announced the appointment of Julio Santoyo as Managing Director of Restaurants – marking a significant milestone in writing the next chapter of the brand. Julio joins from Pret A Manger, bringing 20+ years of experience in one of the most respected food operators in the UK. Starting as a team member after arriving from Spain, he rose through the ranks to become UK Operations Director, overseeing a £700M business across 360 sites and 6,000 team members. Julio said that, “LEON has an important purpose, and it’s one that I completely share. John and I are committed to making it easier to eat and live well. I love food, and I am very curious about what makes people feel and be well. John and I share a lot of values, and at the same time, we bring different skills. I am very happy to be joining John and the brilliant team he is building.” LEON founder and CEO John Vincent called the appointment “a pivotal moment for the company”. “We have long had a spirit of innovation and disruption. We now need to be superb at operations. I would like to make LEON as big as it can be without losing its customer intimacy. This is the challenge Julio and I have set ourselves – for every guest to experience LEON at its best, and to grow as big as we can whilst maintaining soul.” Since launching in 2004, LEON has built a reputation for challenging the status quo – from rethinking fast food to inspiring a generation of better eating. Following John Vincent’s return to the business, at the end of last year, his focus has been to rebuild the company on the foundations of strong operational discipline. The appointment of Julio Santoyo follows a deliberate strategy to build LEON’s “A-team”, including the recent return of CFO Chris Burford, Restaurant Operations Director Nick Scovell and the strengthening of the senior leadership bench.

articles.title: Clemintine Cafe by Anna Higham Opens in October
articles.titleKo: Clemintine Cafe by Anna Higham Opens in October
articles.originalSummary: At Bar Antoine , (Four Seasons Hotel London at Park Lane), the flavours of the French table are being reimagined in liquid form this spring.The bar’s new cocktail menu – Savoir-Boire – draws inspiration from the ingredients, rituals and indulgences of France’s culinary culture; from buttery croissants and nutty Comté to the sharp bite of mustard. At a time when London is rediscovering its appetite for classic French dining, Bar Antoine approaches the tradition from a new angle, translating the flavours of France’s bistrots and boulangeries into unexpected, playful serves. Developed by award-winning Bar Manager Leon Gasco, and under the guidance of the world’s most Michelin-decorated starred chef Yannick Alléno, the cocktail menu pairs emblematic French ingredients with the best of British produce, blurring the line between kitchen and bar. Hero serves include the Croissant Old Fashioned with croissant-infused cognac and Byrrh; the Cornichon Martini with olive oil vodka; the Peach & Mustard Margarita with tequila, peach eau-de-vie and mustard tincture; and the Fig-Affair Paloma finished with a delicate Comté tuille garnish. Translated as “the art of drinking well”, Savoir-Boire is also a celebration of French drinking rituals. The menu unfolds across three chapters beginning with L’Apéro , a tribute to France’s favourite pre-dinner moment, followed by Les Classiques, with reinterpretations of classic cocktails viewed through a French lens. The final chapter, Les Rituels , invites guests to linger while theatrical cocktails are prepared tableside. A new food menu has been designed to accompany the cocktails, featuring classic French ingredients and playful riffs on popular bar snacks. Creative bites include Carabineros prawn toast with tomato and basil; a Pissaladière with caramelised onions, olives and anchovies; and Oeuf Mayo, a crispy soft egg with herb mayonnaise. Larger plates include a twist on the traditional with the ‘ Croque-Antoine :’ the bar’s cult dry-aged Wagyu Antoine Burger and new addition, The CFC ( caviar fried chicken), alongside a rotating selection of French cheeses and artisanal charcuterie, showcasing regional specialities, aged classics and delicately cured meats. Pull up a seat at the central bar, unwind in a cosy corner with plush seating – made with mohair velvets and woven silks by designer Chanan Minassian – or find a spot in the sunshine on the discreet garden terrace, adorned with elegant greenery, accommodating up to 30 guests. With Savoir-Boire , Bar Antoine brings French soul to the heart of London, defined by great drinks, vibrant food, and an undeniable buzz. Santé!

articles.title: Red Robin Moves Forward with $96 Million Refranchising Strategy
articles.titleKo: Red Robin Moves Forward with $96 Million Refranchising Strategy
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . The transactions are a key piece of Red Robin’s First Choice Plan and its efforts to reduce debt and refinance its existing obligations. Red Robin has completed most of a sweeping refranchising initiative that shifted 108 restaurants to three multi-unit operators and brought the casual-dining chain roughly $89.4 million in proceeds. Eight additional locations are scheduled to close by the end of Red Robin’s 2026 fiscal year, pending the transfer of applicable liquor licenses. These restaurant sales are expected to bring in another $6.6 million, pushing the final tally to approximately $96 million. The transactions are a key piece of Red Robin’s First Choice Plan and its efforts to reduce debt and refinance its existing obligations. “Our talented team has made incredible progress in the execution of our First Choice Plan over the past year, and the completion of these refranchising agreements is a critical next step in strengthening our balance sheet as we position our business for sustainable, long-term growth,” CEO Dave Pace said in a statement. Op Burgers is purchasing the largest portion of the portfolio, with an agreement covering 69 restaurants across Kentucky, Indiana, Maryland, Ohio, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, and Virginia for $62.5 million. Kuber Oregon and Kuber Washington acquired 17 Red Robin restaurants in Oregon and Washington for $10 million. Evergreen Dining purchased another 30 locations in Washington and Western Idaho for $23.5 million. Red Robin first disclosed the Evergreen deal in May. The company said at the time that Evergreen’s principals had operated more than 100 restaurants across multiple national brands during nearly three decades in the industry. A few weeks later, Red Robin announced agreements with Op Burgers and Kuber. The chain has been working to improve its financial position and restaurant performance under Pace, who took over as CEO in 2025 and introduced the First Choice Plan. The strategy is built around protecting operational gains, driving traffic, cutting expenses and debt, investing in restaurant facilities and technology, and improving employee performance and retention. “Each of these seasoned operators shares our hospitality-first mindset and brings the resources needed to accelerate growth across these markets, while continuing to deliver an exceptional guest experience,” Pace said. “Importantly, these transactions will advance our efforts to refinance our existing debt and increase our financial flexibility.” Op Burgers said it plans to use its multi-unit operating experience to support employees across its newly acquired restaurants. Kuber pointed to Red Robin’s longstanding following in the Pacific Northwest, and Evergreen said it plans to help grow the brand across Washington and Idaho. Red Robin’s same-store sales rose 1.3 percent in the second quarter, with traffic down just 0.2 percent, the chain’s best traffic performance since early 2023. Traffic turned positive late in the quarter, and restaurant-level operating margin increased 20 basis points to 14.7 percent, its best Q2 result in four years. Red Robin has used value platforms such as Big Yummm, menu innovation, labor efficiencies, technology upgrades, and restaurant refreshes to support the turnaround. The company maintained its 2026 guidance following Q2. The post Red Robin Moves Forward with $96 Million Refranchising Strategy appeared first on FSR magazine .

articles.title: Tigermilk Brings Hacienda Grandeur to the Heart of East London
articles.titleKo: Tigermilk Brings Hacienda Grandeur to the Heart of East London
articles.originalSummary: Their modern South American inspired interior brings life to their largest site to dat e Following its successful opening in May, Tigermilk Spitalfields’s interior has emerged as one of the defining elements of the new flagship restaurant by Alexis and Nina Melikov, the group’s largest site to date. Designed by Studio Leche, Tigermilk’s in-house design studio, the space brings together hacienda-inspired architecture, layered materials and a warm, transportive atmosphere that has become central to the guest experience. Conceived as an escape in the heart of Spitalfields, the ambition was to build an environment that guests would immediately want to stay in, rather than one designed purely to be photographed. Central patios, generous proportions, fountains, handcrafted materials and lush greenery give the space its structure and soul, evoking the kind of environment that takes decades to settle into its surroundings. Antique furniture sits alongside bespoke pieces, and reclaimed terracotta, natural stone, marble and aged timber are used throughout, materials that carry history and wear it well. “People rarely talk about specific design features. They talk about the atmosphere,” adds Alexis. “If people leave believing the space possesses a history, then we have succeeded in creating something that feels authentic rather than constructed.” A considered selection of suppliers and craftspeople underpins the interior. Sogni and Pooky provide the lighting, Pierre Frey and Morris the fabrics and upholstery, and Mandarin Stone the marble and stone surfaces. Flexhouse – responsible for custom joinery, millwork and bespoke fabrication – also contributed to the furniture alongside vintage pieces and Leta, while Resources delivered the decorative wall finishes. Together they bring a layered quality to the space, as though each element has its own provenance and story. With its new 280-cover restaurant, hacienda-inspired interiors and striking luminescent bar stocked with more than 2700 bottles, Tigermilk Spitalfields invites guests into what feels like the brand’s thirteenth home. Through a considered interior scheme full of texture and attention to detail, the restaurant offers a transportive South American-inspired experience designed to engage every sense.

articles.title: Jenki Opens Macha Bar in Soho
articles.titleKo: Jenki Opens Macha Bar in Soho
articles.originalSummary: JENKI will open the doors to its new Soho matcha bar on Thursday 3rd September, bringing the brand to Soho for the first time. Located on Berwick Street, the new opening places JENKI within one of London’s most established food and drink neighbourhoods, joining a growing mix of independent operators in the surrounding streets. The Soho opening comes as JENKI continues its expansion across London, with the brand planning to grow to 11 locations across the capital by the end of 2026. Otto Boyer, co-founder of JENKI, comments: “Soho has been somewhere we’ve wanted to be for a long time. We know from our customers that there has been real demand for us to open here, but it was important to wait for a site that felt right. Berwick Street has such a strong food culture and an amazing mix of independent names around us, so it feels like a very natural home for JENKI and an exciting place for the next bar.” The new bar has been designed by female-led London studio KAI Interiors , whose hospitality projects include Tamila in King’s Cross and Lucy Wong in Soho. Inspired by the Japanese tea fields where JENKI sources its matcha, the interior combines natural clay, timber and fibres with stainless steel, balancing earthy, tactile materials with clean, modern elements. Dark greens, curved forms and dappled lighting further reference the landscape of the tea fields. At the centre of the bar, JENKI’s matcha whisking station makes the preparation process a focal point of the customer experience, with matcha freshly whisked to order in view of guests using the brand’s first harvest matcha sourced directly from Japan. The Soho site will feature intimate seating alcoves, as well as a dedicated retail area showcasing JENKI’s matcha, preparation tools and new lifestyle collection. Founded by Claudia and Otto Boyer in 2020, JENKI began with market stalls and pop ups before opening its first permanent matcha bar in Spitalfields in 2021. The brand has since expanded across London, with locations including Selfridges, Covent Garden, Borough Market, Canary Wharf and Battersea Power Station. The Soho opening forms part of JENKI’s wider growth plans as the brand continues to expand its presence across London this year with new openings in Soho, Liverpool Street, St Paul’s, Fitzrovia, and Marylebone. The Soho bar will officially open on Thursday 3rd September with JENKI’s ‘Matcha on Us’ launch activation, offering complimentary matcha from 10am to 6pm at the new Berwick Street site.

articles.title: The Allure of the Lunch Menu
articles.titleKo: The Allure of the Lunch Menu
articles.originalSummary: For Chef Matt Abé, Chef Patron at London’s newest two Michelin-starred restaurant, Bonheur by Matt Abé , summer is a season tied to memory: ’ summer is tomatoes – the anticipation of watching them grow, the smell you associate with the vine – and fresh fruit, strawberries at their peak .’ It is from these ingredients, flavours and memories that Summer of Bonheur was inspired: a new, three-course, seasonal lunch menu celebrating the essence of British summertime. The menu begins with an Isle of Wight Heirloom Tomato Tart, bringing together vibrant tomatoes, peach and elderflower, finish with a smoked buttermilk and basil sauce. Roast Chicken follows, served with young English peas, charred onions, black garlic, and a roast chicken sauce. To finish, Bonheur’s take on Strawberries and Cream brings together rose, elderflower, lemon verbena, and creamy sour cream ice cream. The Summer of Bonheur is available lunchtimes Thursday – Saturday at £110 per person for three courses Prezzo Fisso Mezzogiorno by Francesco Mazzei Mezzogiorno , the new restaurant by celebrated chef Francesco Mazzei, has launched Prezzo Fisso – a lunch menu brimming with signature southern Italian flavours. The menu starts with an Antipasti of Mozzarella Caprese : vibrant Vesuvio tomatoes with creamy buffalo mozzarella, basil and extra virgin olive oil. A Secondi of Tagliolini Aglio Olio Bottarga and Tuna Crudo follows, with garlic, fiery chilli and gray mullet roe, with a choice of Contorni – choose the spring salad, full with lettuce, cherry tomatoes and radishes, for something light, or the famous Zucchini Fritti , deep fried zucchini sticks. A Strawberry Pannacotta finishes the experience: light vanilla pannacotta with fresh strawberries – a taste of summer, the Italian way. Prezzo Fisso, the new set lunch menu, offers 3 courses at £39 or 2 courses at £32.50 Nobu Signature Lunch Nobu London on Old Park Lane Nobu London on Old Park Lane has introduced Nobu Signature Lunch : a new £40 weekday menu bringing together some of Chef Nobu Matsuhisa’s most celebrated dishes. Designed for those looking to experience the restaurant’s signature flavours in a more accessible format, it’s perfectly suited to the modern lunch hour. Guests begin with a choice of Sashimi Three Ways – featuring Yellowtail Jalapeño, Salmon New Style and Tuna Tataki – or Nobu’s Signature Sushi Selection . This is followed by three of the restaurant’s best-known dishes: Rock Shrimp Tempura with Creamy Spicy Sauce, Black Cod Miso and Beef Tenderloin with Teriyaki or Anticucho sauce, served alongside rice or spicy garlic vegetables. Opened on Old Park Lane in 1997 as the first Nobu outside the USA, the restaurant helped redefine London’s dining scene. Now, the Nobu Signature Lunch offers both a nostalgic return for long-time guests and an invitation for a new generation to experience the dishes that made Nobu a global icon.
