articles.title: Riko’s Pizza Has a Blueprint for Sustainable Growth
articles.titleKo: Riko’s Pizza Has a Blueprint for Sustainable Growth
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . LTOs from Riko's Pizza have performed well this summer. Riko’s Pizza spent much of 2025 putting pieces in place. Now the pizza concept is seeing what those investments can produce. The Stamford, Connecticut-based brand has 13 restaurants and expects to finish 2026 near 18 or 19. Ridgefield, Connecticut, debuted this summer as the 13th unit and has posted record sales, according to CEO Carl Bachmann. Milford, Connecticut, is under construction, along with Holbrook on Long Island and a location in Miami’s Wynwood neighborhood. Those openings form part of a growth pipeline that Bachmann expects to carry significant momentum into 2027. “So the first half of ’26, I think from a growth perspective was really lining up,” Bachmann says. “Getting our team lined up at the end of ’25, then we started lining up new locations, and now we’re starting to open them.” The expansion comes with strong restaurant-level performance. Riko’s posted same-store sales growth of more than 16 percent in 2025. Through July, the brand was running near 8 percent, with its rolling 12-month figure exceeding 10 percent. Traffic has climbed nearly 5 percent. That traffic growth has helped Riko’s resist price increases during a period when restaurant consumers have become more cost conscious. Bachmann sees a distinction between discounting and delivering value, particularly across a pizza category where several major players have struggled to sustain traffic. Riko’s starts with its tavern-style pizza, known for a super-thin crust, with a cheese pizza priced at $11.99. Its menu also gives customers salads, entrées, wings, sliders, and other choices, creating more occasions for families whose members may not all want pizza. “We offer value. We don’t discount much at all, but we also don’t raise our prices and we keep our price point very palatable,” Bachmann says. Riko’s has expanded its menu without sacrificing operational simplicity, giving restaurants opportunities to increase sales through product mix. Bachmann credits that combination of quality, menu diversity, and accessible pricing for helping the chain stand apart. Expansion will come through a mix of company-owned and franchised restaurants. Riko’s is acquiring two Long Island stores from its original franchisee and constructing a third in Holbrook. Bachmann has lived on Long Island for more than 30 years and previously operated restaurants there, giving the company familiarity with the market. The transaction also illustrates how Bachmann views Riko’s development model. The company wants franchise partners capable of multiunit growth, but it does not plan to rely exclusively on franchising. Bachmann prefers having 25 to 50 percent of the system under corporate ownership over time. As of now, the brand comprises eight corporate units and five franchised restaurants. Bachmann estimates that the pipeline is 2:1 in terms of corporate versus operator-led expansion. “I think it’s ultimately important that the franchisor has some skin in the game, and that we’re living in the same world as that franchisee,” Bachmann says. “We have the same labor pressures, the same pricing pressures, the same operational issues, and because of that, and because we’re living in it, we’re solving those problems not only for us but for our franchisees, and I think that’s why it’s so important.” Geographic density is another piece of the plan. Riko’s wants to build clusters of restaurants instead of scattering units across disconnected markets, a strategy Bachmann describes as growing “like a bush, not like a vine.” Connecticut, Long Island, and Westchester County give Riko’s a concentrated presence surrounding Long Island Sound. articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Colony Grill, the Connecticut original known for its Famous Thin-Crust Pizza and signature Hot Oil topping, is continuing its expansion across Hartford County with two new locations planned for Newington and South Windsor, both scheduled to open in 2027. The announcement comes ahead of the opening of Colony Grill’s Glastonbury location and represents another step in the brand’s continued expansion across Connecticut, bringing its Hot Oil Bar Pies to more families and communities throughout the state. “These two towns represent exactly what Colony Grill is about,” said Paul Coniglio, CEO and co-owner of Colony Grill. “We’ve grown this concept around great pizza bringing people together—with teammates coming in after practice, families sharing a Bar Pie on a Tuesday night, or friends catching the game together. Newington and South Windsor have that same strong sense of local pride, and we’re excited not just to open restaurants there, but to become part of the fabric of both towns through the way we serve our guests, support local organizations, and show up for the community.” The Newington location at 3260 Berlin Turnpike, Newington, CT will seat more than 175 guests with a large patio, and introduce Colony Grill’s first-ever fully private dining room. The dedicated space will provide a setting for team dinners, birthday celebrations, and the after-the-game get-togethers that have long been part of the Colony Grill tradition. The restaurant will also feature a full bar with twelve tap lines and several TVs for sports fans in a relaxed atmosphere. “We’re excited to have a space in Newington that gives us even more opportunities to welcome guests in and make them feel at home,” said Ken Martin, COO and co-owner of Colony Grill. “The private dining room gives us a dedicated space to host milestone celebrations, corporate outings, and group dinners while delivering the same great pizza and hospitality that define the Colony Grill experience.” The South Windsor location at 255 Gateway Blvd will bring the same simple, family-friendly Colony Grill experience to Buckland Gateway, a new mixed-use development featuring retail, dining and community spaces. This restaurant will also include Colony’s signature 12-tap bar and multiple TVs, along with seating for approximately 150 guests and an inviting patio offering a welcoming place for nearby residents, families, office workers, and visitors to enjoy Colony’s Famous Hot Oil Bar Pies. “We’re thrilled to welcome Colony Grill to Buckland Gateway,” said Phoebe Sager, Principal of Sager Development. “Colony is exactly the kind of tenant we envisioned for the project—a great Connecticut brand with an incredibly loyal following and a strong commitment to the communities it serves. We believe they will be a terrific addition to South Windsor and an important part of making Buckland Gateway a place where people want to gather, dine and spend time. We’re very excited to have Paul and the entire Colony Grill team here.” The two new locations are part of Colony Grill’s broader expansion across Hartford County and reflect the brand’s continued focus on bringing its distinctive Bar Pie experience into communities where family, sports, and local connection are central. For more information about Colony Grill, visit colonygrill.com. Follow @colonygrill on Instagram and Colony Grill – Newington and Colony Grill – South Windsor on Facebook for more updates. Founded in 1935 in Stamford, Connecticut, Colony Grill is the Home of the Original Hot Oil Bar Pie—a beloved, bar-style pizza best served with its signature, Hot Oil topping. With locations across Connecticut, New York, Virginia, and Florida, Colony Grill is known for its simple menu, welcoming hospitality, and strong ties to the communities it serves. articles.title: Michelin-Recommended Nan Xian Xiao Long to Open New Location in Staten Island Mall
articles.titleKo: Michelin-Recommended Nan Xian Xiao Long to Open New Location in Staten Island Mall
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Queens’ legendary soup dumpling destination is officially coming to Staten Island in 2027. Nan Xiang Xiao Long Bao, the Michelin-recommended culinary institution famous for its handcrafted Shanghainese cuisine, will open its newest location at 280 Marsh Avenue in New Springville, adjacent to the Staten Island Mall. Established in Flushing in 2006, the world-renowned brand has grown from a local favorite into a premier New York City dining destination, celebrated for nine consecutive years by the Michelin Guide for its signature soup dumplings and traditional craftsmanship. “For nearly two decades, guests have traveled to Queens to experience our handcrafted soup dumplings and Shanghainese comfort food,” said Michael Ma, Co-Founder of Nan Xiang Xiao Long Bao. “Every new restaurant gives us the opportunity to introduce another community to the tradition of Xiao Long Bao and the joy of sharing a meal together. We’re excited to become part of the Staten Island community and welcome guests around our table with the same recipes, craftsmanship, and hospitality that have defined Nan Xiang since 2006.” The opening marks Nan Xiang’s highly anticipated debut in the borough, introducing its legendary, handcrafted soup dumplings and authentic Shanghainese cuisine to Staten Island residents, visitors, and the island’s thriving Chinese community. A centerpiece of the new location is its open kitchen. Embodying nearly two decades of culinary excellence, every single xiao long bao is meticulously rolled, filled, and hand-pleated to perfection before being steamed to order—delivering the signature delicate skin, rich broth, and succulent fillings that have solidified Nan Xiang as an iconic New York dining destination. The menu will feature many of the dishes that have earned Nan Xiang national recognition such as the Lucky Six Soup Dumplings, a colorful assortment of six signature soup dumplings featuring distinct fillings and naturally colored wrappers, including Pork, Crab & Pork, Chicken, Pork & Truffle, Luffa Shrimp & Pork, and Scallop & Pork. While handcrafted soup dumplings remain the heart of the menu, Nan Xiang’s offerings extend far beyond the steamer basket. Designed for family-style dining and sharing, it showcases the depth of Shanghainese cuisine alongside regional Chinese specialties, from comforting noodle dishes and wok-fired stir-fries to crispy pan-fried pork buns, scallion pancakes, dim sum favorites, vegetarian offerings, and house-made fruit teas. Guests can also enjoy traditional breakfast specialties served throughout the day, including fried dough sticks paired with warm soybean milk, Northern-style pastries, and other comforting dishes that celebrate the rich flavors and traditions of Chinese cuisine. Nan Xiang Staten Island will accommodate everything from casual lunches and family dinners to celebrations, group gatherings, and convention visitors. The space blends contemporary design with traditional Chinese influences to create a warm and welcoming dining experience. The new 8500-square-foot restaurant will seat 200 guests. For updates, menus, and opening information, visit https://nanxiangxiaolongbao.com/ or follow @nanxiangsoupdumpling on Instagram. The latest installment of its Big Bad Monthly Drop series, Jalapeño Business, is available Sept. 1-30 for $17, including a classic side, and delivers a bold mix of sweet heat, crunch and savory flavor for guests who like their meals with a little attitude. Built on a toasted brioche bun, the Jalapeño Business starts with a seven-ounce beef patty and cheddar cheese, then layers on fresh jalapeño slices, a housemade fried jalapeño popper and housemade raspberry bacon jam. A flash-fried fresh jalapeño finishes the burger with an extra hit, resulting in an over-the-top creation with plenty of crunch and heat. “Jalapeño Business has everything we love about a Bad Daddy’s burger — it’s familiar enough to make sense, but there’s something unexpected in every layer,” said John Masterson, culinary director for Bad Daddy’s Burger Bar. “The housemade raspberry bacon jam adds that sweet and savory balance, while the fresh jalapeños and fried popper bring plenty of heat. The crisp, refreshing Mexican-style lager provides a cool, clean contrast to the burger’s spicy-sweet profile. Available at all Bad Daddy’s locations, September’s drop continues Big Bad’s tradition of introducing unexpected, chef-driven creations straight from a scratch kitchen, giving guests a new reason to visit every month. articles.titleKo: How Chef Adrianne Calvo Turned Family, Flavor, and Loss Into a Miami Restaurant Legacy

Calvo maxed out her credit cards and took the money from her cookbook sales to open Chef Adrianne's Vineyard Restaurant and Bar at the age of 22. Adrianne Calvo realized early on that cooking could create a space of happiness for others. She comes from a culinary-forward family. Some of her earliest memories include running home from school and wondering, “What is Mom cooking today?” The intricacies of the meals her mother was cooking from scratch intrigued her. She’d investigate the various kinds of salsa and the difference between flour and corn tortillas. Looking back, she says she became addicted to the feeling of learning, eating and creating. By high school, Calvo was put into a cooking class by mistake. She calls this the “lightning strike” of her career. “While I was waiting to get my schedule fixed, Johnson & Wales University came in and did a demo of this beautiful stuffed brioche French toast, and it was like I felt myself being put on the right path,” Calvo says. “I went home that day and told my parents, ‘I’m going to be a chef.'” In culinary school, Calvo began entering culinary competitions to help pay off her student debt. She started making a name for herself, and one of the judges encouraged her to compile her recipes into a cookbook. She would go on to become one of the nation’s youngest cookbook authors. “The judge told me, ‘You’re winning based on one thing, and that’s flavor. When you put those recipes together, call that cookbook “Maximum Flavor.”‘ That stayed in the back of my mind,” Calvo says. “Before I know it, I’m in New York City with my family on ‘The Montel Williams Show.'” Despite her early career success, her personal life was upended. Calvo’s younger sister, Jennifer, passed suddenly from a rare form of cancer. Heartbroken, Calvo stopped cooking. Then she saw an ad for an affordable restaurant space in Miami. She felt lightning strike again, like a push from above. She maxed out her credit cards and took the money from her cookbook sales to open Chef Adrianne’s Vineyard Restaurant and Bar at the age of 22. “I had no business experience, just a belief in making really great food and loving to serve people the way my mom served us growing up, with genuine hospitality,” Calvo says. “We opened in an unassuming shopping center, and here we are, 20 years later.” She has watched Miami’s culinary landscape evolve over the years, from the traditional Cuban bakeries she visited as a teenager to the wider array of Colombian, Venezuelan and Caribbean influences that have emerged alongside the city’s growing Latino communities. “The younger generations are culture hungry. They aren’t comfortable with the status quo; they would rather go to smaller restaurants that have a story,” Calvo says. “As storytelling comes forward, we’re going to see more restaurant owners who are open to telling us more about where they came from.” This is seen on Calvo’s own menu. Her lamb chops, for example, are an award-winning recipe dating back to her school days. She says recipes often just pour out of her, and they end up in her cookbooks and on her menu. “If you are real, people want to be a part of what you’re doing,” Calvo says. “Take the audience on a journey, from inception to execution … like, this is a family recipe I am serving to you at my restaurant, or my grandmother taught me this technique, but now I’m incorporating it into this dish to make your experience even more special of an experience.” Giving back for Calvo is not a burden; it’s a responsibility. Inspired by her sister, Calvo is the founder of the Make It Count Foundation, a nonprofit that supports cancer patients and their families. For the 14 th consecutive year, Grimaldi’s Pizzeria is proud to announce its continued partnership with No Kid Hungry. Since 2013, Grimaldi’s annual campaigns have raised more than $1.4 million for No Kid Hungry. Throughout the month of September, guests who donate to No Kid Hungry at Grimaldi’s Pizzeria restaurants nationwide will receive a promotional card that can be redeemed on their next visit. The promotional cards will be gifted in increments of $5 up to a total of $25 per visit. Donations must be made in the restaurant to be eligible to receive the promotional card. For every dollar donated, No Kid Hungry can provide up to 10 meals for hungry children across the country.* “As childhood hunger continues to affect families across the country, we are proud to continue our partnership with No Kid Hungry for a 14 th year,” said Michael Flaum, COO of Grimaldi’s Pizzeria. “This campaign reflects our belief that every child deserves access to meals, and we are grateful to our guests for joining us in supporting programs that help make a meaningful difference in the communities we serve.” *$1 can provide up to 10 meals. Donations help support programs that feed kids; No Kid Hungry does not provide individual meals. Learn more at NoKidHungry.org/OneDollar. MORE TO ENJOY AT GRIMALDI’S In addition to its September No Kid Hungry campaign, Grimaldi’s offers guests more ways to enjoy their signature menu items throughout the week. Stoking Social Hour is available seven days a week from 3 to 5 p.m. at participating locations. While the expert pizza makers stoke the famous coal brick ovens, dine-in guests can enjoy $10 signature cocktails, $3 off starters and salads, $10 off bottles of wine and $2 off beer, wine, spritzes, sangria and mocktails. For a quick weekday meal, Slices ASAP! offers giant red or white pizza slices for $4 from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. Monday through Friday at participating locations. articles.title: Evolve Energy Unlocks CPPA to Power BKUK Restaurants with Renewable Energy
articles.titleKo: Evolve Energy Unlocks CPPA to Power BKUK Restaurants with Renewable Energy
articles.originalSummary: The renewable power will be generated by the Alaska Wind Farm project, the first onshore development of its kind in Dorset Evolve Energy Supply Ltd (Evolve Energy), a licensed UK energy supplier pioneering energy solutions that unlock access to true renewable energy for Industrial & Commercial businesses, has partnered with renewable energy developer Alaska Wind Farm LLP to supply renewable energy from the Alaska Wind Farm near Wareham, Dorset, to BKUK . The collaboration will provide renewable energy to power a proportion of BKUK nationwide restaurants advancing BKUK’s sustainability goals and net zero ambitions. The Alaska Wind Farm comprises four refurbished 2MW Vestas V80 turbines relocated from Belgium, installed at Masters Quarry. As an 8MW wind farm, it generates approximately 17 gigawatt-hours of renewable energy annually. The power generated by the Alaska Wind Farm is secured under a long-term Corporate Power Purchase Agreement (CPPA) with Evolve Energy, which will now enable BKUK to access certifiable renewable energy for a proportion of its operations. James Hall, COO at Evolve Energy, commented: “BKUK has been a valued customer for many years, so it was logical for us to take the unusual step of directly standing behind the CPPA as the contractual party for this impressive renewable project, exclusively matched against their demand. One of the most innovative aspects is the real-time, half-hourly matching of BKUK’s electricity use with the wind farm’s output, enabling non-standard cost savings while helping to reduce emissions. We’re proud to support BKUK integrate more renewable energy into its operations.” Evolve Energy and Alaska Wind Farm LLP were introduced by Sustainable Energy First (SE First), BKUK’s trusted advisory partner commissioned to source a long-term renewable energy solution aligned with BKUK’s energy requirements and sustainability commitments. To help BKUK reduce its reliance on non-renewable energy, SE First partnered with Evolve Energy for its ability to secure direct access to a generator and supply their energy through a CPPA. Evolve Energy worked with Alaska Wind Farm LLP, the renewable developer behind the project, to structure the agreement.
